extraction_notes.note: These notation conventions ($\ll$, $\asymp$, the fixed $a$ and $\epsilon$, $p$, $\phi$, $\mathbf{1}$, gcd, inverses, conjugation, $\ell^2$ norm) are used in almost every later node; edge pass 2 would add hundreds of near-uninformative term edges, so they were left without term edges (orphans) while the more specific notations ($P^-$, $n\sim N$, $z_0,y_0$, $\psi_0$, $S_n$, $\mathrm{Kl}_3$, $F$) were linked.

Section 5 'Paper structure' refers to a dependency diagram that is omitted from the source; the dependencies it shows were recovered from the proofs' \ref's and the optional arguments of the proof environments instead.

Uncited standard facts stated in the introduction (Siegel--Walfisz range under GRH; BV implies most moduli satisfy the asymptotic): TP2 typed theorem (a known prior result), ClP1 kept as claim since it is an immediate consequence rather than a named result.

LP23 is a variant of BFI1 Theorem 0 with an extra $\tau(q)^{B_0}$ weight proved in the paper, kept origin paper; LP19 (Poisson summation) and LP32 (Ramanujan--Weil bound with completion) are standard results the paper re-proves, marked external 'standard (uncited)'.

The heuristic outline (Section 3) and the comparison discussion after Theorems A--C were not made into nodes beyond the numbered outline equations and one explicit claim (ClP2); they argue informally without stating results.

Reference typos in the source: 'Putting together \eqref{eq:D4}, \eqref{eq:DDiag} and \eqref{eq:DDiag}' in the proof of Lemma 16.2 (the second should be eq:DOffDiag), and 'Putting together Lemma 8.12 and Lemma 8.12' before the proof of Proposition 8.1 (should be Lemmas 8.12 and 8.13; that sentence is prose and not a node).

nodes.name: Siegel--Walfisz theorem
nodes.statement_short: Primes are equidistributed in residue classes mod $q$ for $q$ up to a power of $\log x$.

nodes.name: Siegel--Walfisz asymptotic
nodes.statement: \pi(x;q,a)=\Bigl(1+O_A\Bigl(\frac{1}{(\log{x})^A}\Bigr)\Bigr)\frac{\pi(x)}{\phi(q)}.
nodes.label: eq:PNT

nodes.name: Siegel--Walfisz range under GRH
nodes.statement: Under the assumption of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, however, the range when \eqref{eq:PNT} holds can be extended to $q\le x^{1/2}/(\log{x})^B$ for $B=B(A)$ sufficiently large in terms of $A$.
assumptions: Under the assumption of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis
conclusions: the range when \eqref{eq:PNT} holds can be extended to $q\le x^{1/2}/(\log{x})^B$ for $B=B(A)$ sufficiently large in terms of $A$

nodes.name: Montgomery's conjecture
nodes.statement: Moreover, it is conjectured \cite{Montgomery} that \eqref{eq:PNT} should hold for all $q\le x^{1-\epsilon}$.

nodes.name: Bombieri--Vinogradov Theorem
assumptions: for every $A>0$ and $B=B(A)$ sufficiently large in terms of $A$
nodes.statement_short: Primes are equidistributed on average over moduli up to $x^{1/2}/(\log x)^B$, with the error summed with sup over residues.

nodes.name: Bombieri--Vinogradov bound
nodes.statement: \sum_{q\le x^{1/2}/(\log{x})^B}\,\sup_{(a,q)=1}\Bigl|\pi(x;q,a)-\frac{\pi(x)}{\phi(q)}\Bigr|\ll_A\frac{x}{(\log{x})^A}.
nodes.label: eq:BV

nodes.name: Most moduli up to the BV range satisfy the Siegel--Walfisz asymptotic
nodes.statement: If $Q\le x^{1/2}/(\log{x})^B$ then this implies that, for all but $O_A(Q/(\log{x})^A)$ moduli $q\le Q$, we have \eqref{eq:PNT} for all $(a,q)=1$.
conclusions: for all but $O_A(Q/(\log{x})^A)$ moduli $q\le Q$, we have \eqref{eq:PNT} for all $(a,q)=1$

nodes.name: Elliott--Halberstam conjecture
nodes.statement: As with the individual estimate \eqref{eq:PNT}, it is conjectured \cite{ElliottHalberstam} that the range of $q$ in \eqref{eq:BV} can be extended to $q\le x^{1-\epsilon}$.
conclusions: the range of $q$ in \eqref{eq:BV} can be extended to $q\le x^{1-\epsilon}$

nodes.name: Beyond the square-root barrier for Bombieri--Vinogradov
nodes.statement: However, it remains an important outstanding problem in analytic number theory just to extend the range of moduli in \eqref{eq:BV} to $q\le x^{1/2+\epsilon}$, thereby going `beyond the square-root barrier' and producing estimates which are not directly implied by the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis.
nodes.statement_short: Extend the Bombieri--Vinogradov theorem to moduli $q\le x^{1/2+\epsilon}$.

nodes.name: Main theorem: equidistribution for moduli with a conveniently sized factor
nodes.statement: Let $a\in\mathbb{Z}$, let $\epsilon>0$ and let $Q_1,Q_2$ satisfy \begin{align} Q_1Q_2^2&<x^{1-100\epsilon},\\ Q_1^{12}Q_2^7&<x^{4-100\epsilon},\\ Q_1^{20}Q_2^{19}&<x^{10-100\epsilon}. \end{align} Then for every $A>0$ we have \[ \sum_{\substack{q_1\le Q_1\\ (q_1,a)=1}}\sum_{\substack{q_2\le Q_2\\ (q_2,a)=1}}\Bigl|\pi(x;q_1q_2,a)-\frac{\pi(x)}{\phi(q_1q_2)}\Bigr|\ll_{a,\epsilon,A}\frac{x}{(\log{x})^A}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Bombieri--Vinogradov-type bound with absolute values over moduli $q_1q_2$ with $q_1\le Q_1$, $q_2\le Q_2$ under three size constraints, fixed residue $a$.
nodes.label: thrm:MainTheorem

nodes.name: Equidistribution for moduli with a divisor in a convenient range
nodes.statement: Let $a\in\mathbb{Z}$, $0<\delta<1/42$, and $0<\eta<(1-42\delta)/4$ and \[ \mathcal{Q}_{\delta,\eta}:=\Bigl\{q\le x^{1/2+\delta}:\, \exists\, d|q\text{ s.t. }x^{2\delta+\eta}<d<\min\Bigl(\frac{x^{1/10}}{x^{7\delta/5+\eta}},\frac{x^{1/2}}{x^{19\delta+\eta}}\Bigr)\Bigr\}. \] Then for every $A>0$ we have \[ \sum_{\substack{q\in\mathcal{Q}_{\delta,\eta}\\ (q,a)=1}}\Bigl|\pi(x;q,a)-\frac{\pi(x)}{\phi(q)}\Bigr|\ll_{a,\eta,A}\frac{x}{(\log{x})^A}. \]
nodes.statement_short: BV-type bound with absolute values over moduli $q\le x^{1/2+\delta}$ having a divisor in $[x^{2\delta+\eta},\min(x^{1/10-7\delta/5-\eta},x^{1/2-19\delta-\eta})]$.
nodes.label: crllry:BVDivisor

nodes.name: Asymptotic for all but $O(\delta Q)$ moduli
nodes.statement: Let $a\in\mathbb{Z}$, $0<\delta<1/55$, $A>0$ and $Q\le x^{1/2+\delta}$. Then for all but at most $18\delta Q\phi(a)/a$ moduli $q\in [Q,2Q]$ with $(q,a)=1$ we have \[ \pi(x;q,a)=\Bigl(1+O_{a,\delta,A}\Bigl(\frac{1}{(\log{x})^A}\Bigr)\Bigr)\frac{\pi(x)}{\phi(q)}. \]
conclusions: for all but at most $18\delta Q\phi(a)/a$ moduli $q\in [Q,2Q]$ with $(q,a)=1$ we have \[ \pi(x;q,a)=\Bigl(1+O_{a,\delta,A}\Bigl(\frac{1}{(\log{x})^A}\Bigr)\Bigr)\frac{\pi(x)}{\phi(q)}. \]
nodes.statement_short: The prime number theorem in progressions holds for all but $18\delta Q\phi(a)/a$ moduli $q\in[Q,2Q]$, $Q\le x^{1/2+\delta}$.
nodes.label: crllry:MostModuli

nodes.name: Moduli up to $x^{11/21}$
nodes.statement: Let $a\in\mathbb{Z}$, $\epsilon>0$. Then we have for every $A>0$ \[ \sum_{\substack{q_1\le x^{1/21}\\ (q_1,a)=1}}\sum_{\substack{q_2\le x^{10/21-\epsilon} \\ (q_2,a)=1}}\Bigl|\pi(x;q_1q_2,a)-\frac{\pi(x)}{\phi(q_1q_2)}\Bigr|\ll_{a,\epsilon,A}\frac{x}{(\log{x})^A}. \]
nodes.statement_short: BV-type bound for moduli $q_1q_2$ with $q_1\le x^{1/21}$, $q_2\le x^{10/21-\epsilon}$.
nodes.label: crllry:1121

nodes.name: Bombieri--Friedlander--Iwaniec theorem for all moduli slightly beyond $x^{1/2}$
nodes.statement: Let $a\in\mathbb{Z}$, $\delta>0$ and $Q=x^{1/2+\delta}$. Then we have \[ \sum_{\substack{q\in[Q,2Q]\\(q,a)=1}}\Bigl|\pi(x;q,a)-\frac{\pi(x)}{\phi(q)}\Bigr|\ll_a\delta^2\frac{x}{\log{x}}+\frac{x(\log\log{x})^{O(1)}}{(\log{x})^3}. \]
nodes.label: nthrm:BFI2

nodes.name: Bombieri--Friedlander--Iwaniec theorem for well-factorable weights
nodes.statement: Let $A>0$ and $\lambda_d$ be a well-factorable sequence of level $Q<x^{4/7-\epsilon}$. Then we have \[ \sum_{\substack{q\le Q\\ (q,a)=1}}\lambda_q\Bigl(\pi(x;q,a)-\frac{\pi(x)}{\phi(q)}\Bigr)\ll_{a,A,\epsilon}\frac{x}{(\log{x})^A}. \]
assumptions: $\lambda_d$ be a well-factorable sequence of level $Q<x^{4/7-\epsilon}$
nodes.label: nthrm:BFI

nodes.name: Zhang--Polymath theorem for smooth moduli
nodes.statement: Let $a\in\mathbb{Z}$, $0<\delta<7/300$ and $Q=x^{1/2+\delta}$. Then there is a constant $\eta=\eta(\delta)>0$ such that for every $A>0$ \[ \sum_{\substack{q\le Q \\(q,a)=1\\ p|q\Rightarrow p\le x^\eta}}\Bigl|\pi(x;q,a)-\frac{\pi(x)}{\phi(q)}\Bigr|\ll_A\frac{x}{(\log{x})^A}. \]
conclusions: there is a constant $\eta=\eta(\delta)>0$ such that for every $A>0$ \[ \sum_{\substack{q\le Q \\(q,a)=1\\ p|q\Rightarrow p\le x^\eta}}\Bigl|\pi(x;q,a)-\frac{\pi(x)}{\phi(q)}\Bigr|\ll_A\frac{x}{(\log{x})^A}. \]
nodes.label: nthrm:Zhang

nodes.name: Theorem C for fixed residue up to $x^{11/20}$
nodes.statement: Indeed, for a fixed residue class, Theorem \ref{thrm:MainTheorem} implies that Theorem \ref{nthrm:Zhang} holds with moduli of size up to $x^{11/20-\epsilon}$.
conclusions: Theorem \ref{nthrm:Zhang} holds with moduli of size up to $x^{11/20-\epsilon}$

nodes.name: Outline: target sum for five-factor convolutions
nodes.statement: \sum_{q\sim Q}c_q\sum_{n_1\sim N_1}\alpha_{n_1}\sum_{n_2\sim N_2}\beta_{n_2}\sum_{n_3\sim N_3}\Bigl(\mathbf{1}_{n_1n_2n_3\equiv a\Mod{q}}-\frac{\mathbf{1}_{(n_1n_2n_3,q)=1}}{\phi(q)}\Bigr)
nodes.label: eq:OverallTarget

nodes.name: Outline: sum after Cauchy--Schwarz
nodes.statement: \sum_{q\sim Q}\sum_{n_3,n_3'\sim N_3}\sum_{\substack{n_2,n_2'\sim N_2\\ n_2n_3\equiv n_2'n_3'\Mod{q}}}\beta_{n_2}\beta_{n_2'}\sum_{\substack{n_1\sim N_1\\ n_1n_2n_3\equiv a\Mod{q}}}1.
nodes.label: eq:OverallTarget2

nodes.name: Outline: exponential sum after completion
nodes.statement: \sum_{r\sim N_2N_3/Q}\sum_{n_3,n_3'\sim N_3}\sum_{\substack{n_2,n_2'\sim N_2\\ n_2n_3\equiv n_2'n_3'\Mod{r}}}\beta_{n_2}\beta_{n_2'}\sum_{h\sim Q/N_1}e\Bigl(\frac{ah\overline{n_2'n_3'}}{n_2n_3}\Bigr).
nodes.label: eq:OverallTarget3

nodes.name: Outline: BFI sum after second Cauchy--Schwarz
nodes.statement: \sum_{r\sim N_2N_3/Q}\,\sum_{n\sim N_2N_3}\sum_{n_2'\sim N_2}\Bigl|\sum_{h\sim Q/N_1}\sum_{\substack{n_3'\sim N_3\\ n_2'n_3'\equiv n\Mod{r}}}\beta_{n_2'}e\Bigl(\frac{ah\overline{n_2'n_3'}}{n}\Bigr)\Bigr|^2.
nodes.label: eq:OverallTarget4

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 1.2
nodes.statement: For notational convenience set $D_1:=x^{2\delta+\eta}/2$ and $D_2:=\min(x^{1/10-7\delta/5-\eta},x^{1/2-19\delta-\eta})$. By considering the $d$ in dyadic ranges we see that \begin{align*} \mathcal{Q}_{\delta,\eta}&\subseteq \bigcup_{\substack{D=2^j\\ D_1\le D\le D_2}}\Bigl\{q\le x^{1/2+\delta}:\,\exists d|q \text{ s.t. }d\in[D,2D]\Bigr\}\\ &=\bigcup_{\substack{D=2^j\\ D_1\le D\le D_2}}\Bigl\{q_1q_2\le x^{1/2+\delta}:\,q_1\in[D,2D]\Bigr\}. \end{align*} We now set $Q_1:=2D$ and $Q_2:=x^{1/2+\delta}/D$, noting that if $q_1q_2\le x^{1/2+\delta}$ and $q_1\in[D,2D]$ then $q_1\le Q_1$ and $q_2\le Q_2$. If $D_1\le D \le D_2$ we have \begin{align*} Q_1Q_2^2&=2\frac{x^{1+2\delta}}{D}\ll x^{1-\eta},\\ Q_1^{12}Q_2^7&=2^{12}D^5 x^{7/2+7\delta}\ll x^{4-5\eta},\\ Q_1^{20}Q_2^{19}&=2^{20}D x^{19/2+19\delta}\ll x^{10-\eta}. \end{align*} Thus, by the union bound and applying Theorem \ref{thrm:MainTheorem} (with $\epsilon=\eta/101$) we see that \begin{align*} \sum_{\substack{q\in \mathcal{Q}_{\delta,\eta}\\ (q,a)=1}}\Bigl|\pi(x;q,a)-\frac{\pi(x)}{\phi(q)}\Bigr|&\ll (\log{x})\sup_{D_1\le D\le D_2}\sum_{q_1\le 2D}\sum_{q_2\le x^{1/2+\delta}/D}\Bigl|\pi(x;q_1q_2,a)-\frac{\pi(x)}{\phi(q_1q_2)}\Bigr|\\ &\ll_{a, A,\eta} \frac{x}{(\log{x})^A}.\qedhere \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Cover $\mathcal{Q}_{\delta,\eta}$ by dyadic ranges of the divisor and apply Theorem 1.1 to each with $Q_1=2D$, $Q_2=x^{1/2+\delta}/D$.

nodes.name: Dyadic covering of the moduli set
nodes.statement_short: Set $D_1,D_2$ and cover $\mathcal{Q}_{\delta,\eta}$ by dyadic divisor ranges.

nodes.name: Check constraints of Theorem 1.1
nodes.statement_short: Choose $Q_1,Q_2$ and verify (1.3)--(1.5).

nodes.name: Apply Theorem 1.1
nodes.statement_short: Union bound plus Theorem 1.1 give the result.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 1.3
nodes.statement: We let $\eta=\epsilon\delta$. Since $0<\delta<1/55$, we see that any $q\sim Q$ with $q\notin \mathcal{Q}_{\delta,\eta}$ must be the product $m_1m_2$ with $m_1<x^{(2+\epsilon)\delta}$ and $P^-(m_2)\ge x^{1/10-(7/5+\epsilon)\delta}\ge (Q/m_1)^{1/7}$, where we use $P^-(m)$ to denote the smallest prime factor of $m$. We recall that as $t\rightarrow\infty$ \[ \sum_{\substack{n\le t\\ P^-(n)\ge t^\gamma}}1=\Bigl(\omega\Bigl(\frac{1}{\gamma}\Bigr)+o_\gamma(1)\Bigr)\frac{t}{\gamma\log{t}} , \] where $\omega(u)$ is the Buchtab function, which is piecewise continuous and satisfies $\omega(7)< 4/7$. Thus we see that for $\epsilon$ small enough and $x$ large enough \begin{align*} \sum_{\substack{q\in [Q,2Q]\backslash\mathcal{Q}_{\delta,\eta}\\ (q,a)=1}}1\le \sum_{\substack{m_1\le x^{(2+\epsilon)\delta} \\ (m_1,a)=1}}\sum_{\substack{Q/m_1\le m_2\le 2Q/m_1\\ P^-(m_2)\ge (Q/m_1)^{1/7}}}1&= \sum_{\substack{m_1\le x^{(2+\epsilon)\delta}\\ (m_1,a)=1}}\frac{(7\omega(7)+o(1))Q}{m_1\log(Q/m_1)}\\ &\le \frac{\phi(a)}{a}\frac{(4+o(1))Q(2+\epsilon)\delta}{1/2-(2+\epsilon)\delta}\le 18\frac{\phi(a)\delta Q}{a}. \end{align*} By Corollary \ref{crllry:BVDivisor}, for all but $O(Q/\log^A{x})$ moduli $q\in\mathcal{Q}_{\delta,\eta}$ with $(q,a)=1$ we have \[ \pi(x;q,a)=\frac{\pi(x)}{\phi(q)}+O_{a,A,\delta}\Bigl(\frac{x}{(\log{x})^{A}}\Bigr). \] Putting this all together gives the result.
nodes.statement_short: Count moduli without a convenient divisor via the Buchstab function ($\omega(7)<4/7$); the rest are handled by Corollary 1.2.

nodes.name: Structure of excluded moduli
nodes.statement: We let $\eta=\epsilon\delta$. Since $0<\delta<1/55$, we see that any $q\sim Q$ with $q\notin \mathcal{Q}_{\delta,\eta}$ must be the product $m_1m_2$ with $m_1<x^{(2+\epsilon)\delta}$ and $P^-(m_2)\ge x^{1/10-(7/5+\epsilon)\delta}\ge (Q/m_1)^{1/7}$, where we use $P^-(m)$ to denote the smallest prime factor of $m$.
nodes.statement_short: Moduli outside $\mathcal{Q}_{\delta,\eta}$ factor as $m_1m_2$ with $m_2$ rough.

nodes.name: Recall rough-number count
nodes.statement:
We recall that as $t\rightarrow\infty$
\[
\sum_{\substack{n\le t\\ P^-(n)\ge t^\gamma}}1=\Bigl(\omega\Bigl(\frac{1}{\gamma}\Bigr)+o_\gamma(1)\Bigr)\frac{t}{\gamma\log{t}} ,
\]
where $\omega(u)$ is the Buchtab function, which is piecewise continuous and satisfies $\omega(7)< 4/7$.
nodes.statement_short: Recall the count of rough numbers via the Buchstab function.

nodes.name: Bound exceptional moduli
nodes.statement_short: At most $18\phi(a)\delta Q/a$ moduli lie outside $\mathcal{Q}_{\delta,\eta}$.

nodes.name: Apply Corollary 1.2
nodes.statement:
By Corollary \ref{crllry:BVDivisor}, for all but $O(Q/\log^A{x})$ moduli $q\in\mathcal{Q}_{\delta,\eta}$ with $(q,a)=1$ we have 
\[
\pi(x;q,a)=\frac{\pi(x)}{\phi(q)}+O_{a,A,\delta}\Bigl(\frac{x}{(\log{x})^{A}}\Bigr).
\] 
Putting this all together gives the result.
nodes.statement_short: Corollary 1.2 handles moduli in $\mathcal{Q}_{\delta,\eta}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 1.4
nodes.statement: This is immediate from Theorem \ref{thrm:MainTheorem} taking $Q_1=x^{1/21}$, $Q_2=x^{10/21-100\epsilon}$, and then redefining $\epsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: Specialize Theorem 1.1 to $Q_1=x^{1/21}$, $Q_2=x^{10/21-100\epsilon}$.

nodes.name: Vinogradov and big-O notation
nodes.statement: We will use the Vinogradov $\ll$ and $\gg$ asymptotic notation, and the big oh $O(\cdot)$ and $o(\cdot)$ asymptotic notation.

nodes.name: Asymptotic equivalence notation
nodes.statement: $f\asymp g$ will denote the conditions $f\ll g$ and $g\ll f$ both hold.

nodes.name: Fixed residue class $a$
nodes.statement: We will view $a$ (the residue class we count arithmetic functions in to different moduli $q$) as a fixed positive integer throughout the paper, and any constants implied by asymptotic notation will be allowed to depend on $a$ from this point onwards.

nodes.name: Fixed small parameter $\epsilon$
nodes.statement: Similarly, throughout the paper, we will let $\epsilon$ be a single fixed small real number; $\epsilon=10^{-100}$ would probably suffice.

nodes.name: Prime letter $p$
nodes.statement: The letter $p$ will always be reserved to denote a prime number.

nodes.name: Totient, exponential, divisor and Mobius functions
nodes.statement: We use $\phi$ to denote the Euler totient function, $e(x):=e^{2\pi i x}$ the complex exponential, $\tau_k(n)$ the $k$-fold divisor function, $\mu(n)$ the M\"obius function.

nodes.name: Smallest and largest prime factors; Fourier transform
nodes.statement: We let $P^-(n)$, $P^+(n)$ denote the smallest and largest prime factors of $n$ respectively, and $\hat{f}$ denote the Fourier transform of $f$ over $\mathbb{R}$ - i.e. $\hat{f}(\xi)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(t)e(-\xi t)dt$.

nodes.name: Indicator function
nodes.statement: We use $\mathbf{1}$ to denote the indicator function of a statement.

nodes.name: gcd notation
nodes.statement: We will use $(a,b)$ to denote $\gcd(a,b)$ when it does not conflict with notation for ordered pairs.

nodes.name: Modular inverse $\overline{n}$
nodes.statement: For $(n,q)=1$, we will use $\overline{n}$ to denote the inverse of the integer $n$ modulo $q$; the modulus will be clear from the context.

nodes.name: Complex conjugation bar
nodes.statement: Occasionally we will also use $\overline{\lambda}$ to denote complex conjugation; the distinction of the usage should be clear from the context.

nodes.name: $\ell^2$ norm of a sequence
nodes.statement: For a complex sequence $\alpha_{n_1,\dots,n_k}$, $\|\alpha\|_2$ will denote the $\ell^2$ norm $\|\alpha\|_2=(\sum_{n_1,\dots,n_k}|\alpha_{n_1,\dots,n_k}|^2)^{1/2}$.

nodes.name: Dyadic notation $n\sim N$
nodes.statement: We use the notation $n\sim N$ to denote the conditions $N<n\le 2N$.

nodes.name: Parameters $z_0$ and $y_0$
nodes.statement: We will let $z_0:=x^{1/(\log\log{x})^3}$ and $y_0:=x^{1/\log\log{x}}$ two parameters depending on $x$, which we will think of as a large quantity.

nodes.name: Smooth bump function $\psi_0$
nodes.statement: We will let $\psi_0:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ denote a fixed smooth function supported on $[1/2,5/2]$ which is identically equal to $1$ on the interval $[1,2]$ and satisfies the derivative bounds $\|\psi_0^{(j)}\|_\infty\ll (4^j j!)^2$ for all $j\ge 0$.
differentia: identically equal to $1$ on the interval $[1,2]$
satisfies the derivative bounds $\|\psi_0^{(j)}\|_\infty\ll (4^j j!)^2$ for all $j\ge 0$

nodes.name: Siegel-Walfisz condition
nodes.statement: We say that a complex sequence $\alpha_n$ satisfies the \textbf{Siegel-Walfisz condition} if for every $d\ge 1$, $q\ge 1$ and $(a,q)=1$ and every $A>1$ we have \begin{equation} \Bigl|\sum_{\substack{n\sim N\\ n\equiv a\Mod{q}\\ (n,d)=1}}\alpha_n-\frac{1}{\phi(q)}\sum_{\substack{n\sim N\\ (n,d q)=1}}\alpha_n\Bigr|\ll_A \frac{N\tau(d)^{B_0}}{(\log{N})^A}. \end{equation}
differentia: for every $d\ge 1$, $q\ge 1$ and $(a,q)=1$ and every $A>1$ we have
nodes.statement_short: $\alpha_n$ is equidistributed in residue classes to small moduli, coprime to $d$, with saving any power of $\log N$.

nodes.name: Siegel-Walfisz bound
nodes.statement: \Bigl|\sum_{\substack{n\sim N\\ n\equiv a\Mod{q}\\ (n,d)=1}}\alpha_n-\frac{1}{\phi(q)}\sum_{\substack{n\sim N\\ (n,d q)=1}}\alpha_n\Bigr|\ll_A \frac{N\tau(d)^{B_0}}{(\log{N})^A}.
nodes.label: eq:SiegelWalfisz

nodes.name: Basic sequences satisfying the Siegel-Walfisz condition
nodes.statement: We note that $\alpha_n$ certainly satisfies the Siegel-Walfisz condition if $\alpha_n=1$, if $\alpha_n=\mu(n)$ or if $\alpha_n$ is the indicator function of the primes.
conclusions: $\alpha_n$ certainly satisfies the Siegel-Walfisz condition if $\alpha_n=1$, if $\alpha_n=\mu(n)$ or if $\alpha_n$ is the indicator function of the primes

nodes.name: Discrepancy weights $S_n$ and $S_d(z)$
also_stated_at:
We recall that here (and throughout the paper) $S_n$ is defined by
\[
S_n:=\mathbf{1}_{n\equiv a\Mod{q_1q_2}}-\frac{1}{\phi(q_1q_2)}\mathbf{1}_{(n,q_1q_2)=1}.
\]

We recall that $S_n$ is defined by
\[
S_n:=\mathbf{1}_{n\equiv a\Mod{q_1q_2}}-\frac{\mathbf{1}_{(n,q_1q_2)=1}}{\phi(q_1q_2)}.
\]

We recall that here (and throughout the paper) $S_n$ is defined by
\[
S_n:=\mathbf{1}_{n\equiv a\Mod{q_1q_2}}-\frac{1}{\phi(q_1q_2)}\mathbf{1}_{(n,q_1q_2)=1}
\]
nodes.statement_short: $S_n$ is the discrepancy of $n$ in the progression $a$ mod $q_1q_2$; $S_d(z)$ sums $S_{dn}$ over $z$-rough $n\sim x/d$.

nodes.name: Type II estimate (sieve form)
nodes.statement: Let $Q_1,Q_2 $ satisfy \eqref{eq:Cons1} and \eqref{eq:Cons2}. Let $P_1,\dots, P_J\ge x^{1/7+10\epsilon}$ be such that $P_1\cdots P_J\ll x$ and \[ x^{3/7+\epsilon}\le\prod_{j\in\mathcal{J}}P_j\le x^{4/7-\epsilon} \] for some subset $\mathcal{J}\subseteq\{1,\dots,J\}$. Then we have \[ \sum_{q_1\sim Q_1}\sum_{\substack{q_2\sim Q_2\\ (q_1q_2,a)=1}}\Bigl|\mathop{\sideset{}{^*}\sum}_{\substack{p_1,\dots,p_J\\ p_i\sim P_i\,\forall i}}S_{p_1\cdots p_J}(p_J)\Bigr|\ll_A\frac{x}{(\log{x})^A}. \] Here $\sum^*$ indicates that the summation is restricted by $O(1)$ inequalities of the form $p_1^{\alpha_1}\cdots p_J^{\alpha_J}\le B$. The implied constant may depend on all such exponents $\alpha_i$, but none of the quantities $B$.
assumptions: $P_1,\dots, P_J\ge x^{1/7+10\epsilon}$ be such that $P_1\cdots P_J\ll x$
nodes.statement_short: Products of primes with a subproduct in $[x^{3/7+\epsilon},x^{4/7-\epsilon}]$ are equidistributed (sieve-weighted form).
nodes.label: prpstn:TypeII2

nodes.name: Sieve asymptotics
nodes.statement: Let $A>0$. Let $x^{3/7+\epsilon}\ge P_1\ge \dots \ge P_r\ge x^{1/7+10\epsilon}$ be such that $P_1\cdots P_r\le x^{2/3}$ and such that either $r=1$ or $P_r\le x^{1/4+\epsilon}$. Let $Q_1,Q_2$ satisfy \eqref{eq:Cons1}, \eqref{eq:Cons2} and \eqref{eq:Cons3}. Then we have \[ \sum_{q_1\sim Q_1}\sum_{\substack{q_2\sim Q_2\\ (q_1q_2,a)=1}} \Bigl|\mathop{\sideset{}{^*}\sum}_{\substack{p_1,\dots,p_r\\ p_i\sim P_i\,\forall i}} S_{p_1\cdots p_r}(x^{1/7+10\epsilon})\Bigr|\ll_{A}\frac{x}{(\log{x})^A}. \] Here $\sum^*$ means that the summation is restricted to $O(1)$ inequalities of the form $p_1^{\alpha_1}\cdots p_r^{\alpha_r}\le B$ for some constants $\alpha_1,\dots \alpha_r$. The implied constant may depend on all such exponents $\alpha_i$, but none of the quantities $B$. Moreover, we also have the related estimate \[ \sum_{q_1\sim Q_1}\sum_{\substack{q_2\sim Q_2\\ (q_1q_2,a)=1}} \Bigl|S_{1}(x^{1/7+10\epsilon})\Bigr|\ll_{A}\frac{x}{(\log{x})^A}. \]
assumptions: $x^{3/7+\epsilon}\ge P_1\ge \dots \ge P_r\ge x^{1/7+10\epsilon}$ be such that $P_1\cdots P_r\le x^{2/3}$ and such that either $r=1$ or $P_r\le x^{1/4+\epsilon}$
conclusions: \sum_{q_1\sim Q_1}\sum_{\substack{q_2\sim Q_2\\ (q_1q_2,a)=1}} \Bigl|\mathop{\sideset{}{^*}\sum}_{\substack{p_1,\dots,p_r\\ p_i\sim P_i\,\forall i}} S_{p_1\cdots p_r}(x^{1/7+10\epsilon})\Bigr|\ll_{A}\frac{x}{(\log{x})^A}.
nodes.statement_short: Sieve-weighted sums $S_{p_1\cdots p_r}(x^{1/7+10\epsilon})$ with few large primes are equidistributed on average over $q_1q_2$.
nodes.label: prpstn:SieveAsymptotic

nodes.name: Numbers with 4 or more prime factors
nodes.statement: Let $A>0$. Let $J\ge 4$ and $P_1\ge\dots\ge P_J\ge x^{1/7+10\epsilon}$ with $P_1\cdots P_J\asymp x$. Let $Q_1,Q_2$ satisfy \eqref{eq:Cons1} and \eqref{eq:Cons2}. Then we have \[ \sum_{q_1\sim Q_1}\sum_{\substack{q_2\sim Q_2\\ (q_1q_2,a)=1}}\Bigl|\mathop{\sideset{}{^*}\sum}_{\substack{p_1,\dots,p_J\\ p_i\sim P_i\forall i}}S_{p_1\cdots p_J}\Bigr|\ll_{A}\frac{x}{(\log{x})^A}. \] Here $\sum^*$ indicates that the summation is restricted by $O(1)$ inequalities of the form $p_1^{\alpha_1} \cdots p_J^{\alpha_J}\le B$. The implied constant may depend on all such exponents $\alpha_i$, but none of the quantities $B$.
assumptions: $J\ge 4$ and $P_1\ge\dots\ge P_J\ge x^{1/7+10\epsilon}$ with $P_1\cdots P_J\asymp x$
conclusions: \sum_{q_1\sim Q_1}\sum_{\substack{q_2\sim Q_2\\ (q_1q_2,a)=1}}\Bigl|\mathop{\sideset{}{^*}\sum}_{\substack{p_1,\dots,p_J\\ p_i\sim P_i\forall i}}S_{p_1\cdots p_J}\Bigr|\ll_{A}\frac{x}{(\log{x})^A}.
nodes.statement_short: Products of $J\ge4$ primes all larger than $x^{1/7+10\epsilon}$ are equidistributed on average over $q_1q_2$.
nodes.label: prpstn:4Primes

nodes.name: Numbers with three prime factors
nodes.statement: Let $A>0$ and let $P_1,P_2,P_3\in [x^{1/4},x^{3/7+\epsilon}]$ with $P_1P_2P_3\asymp x$. Then we have \[ \sum_{q_1\sim Q_1}\sum_{\substack{q_2\sim Q_2\\ (q_1q_2,a)=1}}\Bigl|\mathop{\sideset{}{^*}\sum}_{\substack{p_1,p_2,p_3\\ p_i\sim P_i\forall i}}S_{p_1p_2p_3}\Bigr|\ll_A \frac{x}{(\log{x})^A}. \] Here $\sum^*$ means that the summation is restricted to $O(1)$ inequalities of the form $p_1^{\alpha_1}p_2^{\alpha_2} p_3^{\alpha_3}\le B$ for some constants $\alpha_1,\alpha_2, \alpha_3$. The implied constant may depend on all such exponents $\alpha_i$, but none of the quantities $B$.
nodes.statement_short: Products of three primes in $[x^{1/4},x^{3/7+\epsilon}]$ are equidistributed on average over $q_1q_2$.
nodes.label: prpstn:3Primes

nodes.name: Buchstab's identity
nodes.statement: Let $z_1<z_2$. Then \[ S_d(z_2)=S_d(z_1)-\sum_{z_1<p\le z_2}S_{d p}(p) \]

nodes.name: Proof of Buchstab's identity
nodes.statement: This is inclusion-exclusion based on the smallest prime factor of $n$ in the sum in $S_d(z)$.
nodes.statement_short: Inclusion-exclusion on the smallest prime factor.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.1 assuming Propositions 7.1--7.4
nodes.statement:
We first establish some notation. Let $z_1,z_2,z_3$ be defined in terms of $x$ by egin{align*} z_1&:= x^{1/7+10\epsilon},&\qquad z_2&:=x^{3/7+\epsilon},&\qquad z_3:=x^{4/7-\epsilon}. \end{align*} For the purposes of this section (but this section only), we assume that the symbols $r,s,t,u,v$ represent prime numbers, in the same manner that we use the symbol $p$. Our goal is to estimate egin{equation} \sum_{q_1\sim Q_1}\sum_{\substack{q_2\sim Q_2\ (q_1q_2,a)=1}}|S_1(2x^{1/2})|=\sum_{q_1\sim Q_1}\sum_{\substack{q_2\sim Q_2\ (q_1q_2,a)=1}}\Bigl|\sum_{\substack{p\sim x\ p\equiv a\Mod{q_1q_2}}}1- rac{1}{\phi(q)}\sum_{\substack{p\sim x\ (p,q_1q_2)=1}}1\Bigr| \end{equation} by decomposing $S_1(2x^{1/2})$ into terms which can be handled by one of Proposition ef{prpstn:TypeII2}, Proposition ef{prpstn:SieveAsymptotic}, Proposition ef{prpstn:4Primes} or Proposition ef{prpstn:3Primes}. By Buchstab's identity egin{align} S_1(2x^{1/2})&=S_1(z_1)-\sum_{z_1< p\le z_2}S_p(p)-\sum_{z_2< p\le 2x^{1/2}}S_p(p). \end{align} By Proposition ef{prpstn:SieveAsymptotic}, the first term on the right hand side of \eqref{eq:Decomp0} makes a negligible contribution to \eqref{eq:Target} (i.e. a contribution of size $O_{A}(x/(\log{x})^A)$ when summed with absolute values over $q_1$ and $q_2$). Similarly, by Proposition ef{prpstn:TypeII2}, the last term also contributes negligibly. Thus we are left to consider the middle term. We note that if $p\in[2x^{1/3},z_2]$ then $S_p(p)$ just counts products of two primes, and so is equal to $S_p(x^{1/2+\epsilon}/p^{1/2})$. Thus, applying Buchstab's identity again, we have egin{align} \sum_{z_1< p\le z_2}S_p(p)&=\sum_{z_1x^{1/4}}}S_{p r}(r). \end{align} (We have simplified some of the conditions of summation above.) By Proposition ef{prpstn:SieveAsymptotic}, the first term in \eqref{eq:Decomp1} contributes negligibly to \eqref{eq:Target}. By Proposition ef{prpstn:TypeII2}, the third term also contributes negligibly. Thus we are left to consider the remaining three terms of \eqref{eq:Decomp1}. We first consider the final term of \eqref{eq:Decomp1}. Since $p r^3>2x$ this counts products of exactly three primes. Specifically \[ \sum_{\substack{z_1< r\le p\le z_2\ z_3

nodes.statement_short: Harman-sieve decomposition: iterate Buchstab's identity and route each term to Propositions 7.1--7.4.

nodes.statement_short: Introduce $z_1,z_2,z_3$ and prime letters $r,s,t,u,v$.

nodes.statement_short: Buchstab gives (7.2); outer terms handled by Props 7.2 and 7.1.

Thus, applying Buchstab's identity again, we have \begin{align} \sum_{z_1< p\le z_2}S_p(p)&=\sum_{z_1x^{1/4}}}S_{p r}(r). \end{align} (We have simplified some of the conditions of summation above.)

By Proposition \ref{prpstn:TypeII2}, the third term also contributes negligibly. Thus we are left to consider the remaining three terms of \eqref{eq:Decomp1}.

nodes.statement_short: Final term counts products of three primes; Prop 7.4 applies.

nodes.name: Fourth term
nodes.statement_short: Buchstab (7.4); pieces handled by Props 7.2 and 7.3.

nodes.name: Second term
nodes.statement_short: Two more Buchstab steps (7.5)--(7.7); pieces handled by Props 7.2 and 7.3.

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement:
Putting everything together, we find that
\[
\sum_{q_1\sim Q_1}\sum_{\substack{q_2\sim Q_2\\ (q_1q_2,a)=1}}|S_1(2x^{1/2})|\ll_A\frac{x}{(\log{x})^A},
\]
as required.
nodes.statement_short: All terms are negligible, giving the bound.

nodes.name: Target sum (7.1)
nodes.statement: \sum_{q_1\sim Q_1}\sum_{\substack{q_2\sim Q_2\\ (q_1q_2,a)=1}}|S_1(2x^{1/2})|=\sum_{q_1\sim Q_1}\sum_{\substack{q_2\sim Q_2\\ (q_1q_2,a)=1}}\Bigl|\sum_{\substack{p\sim x\\ p\equiv a\Mod{q_1q_2}}}1-\frac{1}{\phi(q)}\sum_{\substack{p\sim x\\ (p,q_1q_2)=1}}1\Bigr|
nodes.label: eq:Target

nodes.statement: \sum_{z_1< p\le z_2}S_p(p)&=\sum_{z_1x^{1/4}}}S_{p r}(r).
nodes.label: eq:Decomp1

nodes.statement: \sum_{\substack{z_1< r\le p\le z_2\\ p r\le z_2}}S_{p r}( r)&=\sum_{\substack{z_1< r\le p\le z_2\\ p r\le z_2}}S_{p r}(z_1)-\sum_{\substack{z_1< s\le r\le p\le z_2\\ p r\le z_2}}S_{p r s}(s).
nodes.label: eq:Decomp2

nodes.name: Decomposition (7.6)
nodes.statement: \sum_{\substack{z_1< s\le r\le p\le z_2\\ p r\le z_2}}S_{p r s}(s)&=\sum_{\substack{z_1< s\le r\le p\le z_2\\ p r\le z_2}}S_{p r s}(z_1)-\sum_{\substack{z_1< t\le s\le r\le p\le z_2\\ p r\le z_2}}S_{p r s t}(t)

nodes.statement: \sum_{\substack{z_1< t\le s\le r\le p\le z_2\\ p r\le z_2}}S_{p r s t}(t)=\sum_{\substack{z_1< t\le s\le r\le p\le z_2\\ p r\le z_2\\ p r s t u\sim x}}S_{p r s t u}+\sum_{\substack{z_1< t\le s\le r\le p\le z_2\\ p r\le z_2\\ t< u\le v\\ p r s t u v\sim x}}S_{p r s t u v}.
nodes.label: eq:Decomp6

nodes.name: Type II estimate
nodes.statement: Let $A>0$ and let $Q_1,Q_2 $ satisfy \eqref{eq:Cons1} and \eqref{eq:Cons2}. Let $P_1,\dots, P_J\ge x^{1/7+10\epsilon}$ be such that $P_1\cdots P_J\asymp x$ and \[ x^{3/7+\epsilon}\le\prod_{j\in\mathcal{J}}P_j\le x^{4/7-\epsilon} \] for some subset $\mathcal{J}\subseteq\{1,\dots,J\}$. Then we have \[ \sum_{q_1\sim Q_1}\sum_{\substack{q_2\sim Q_2\\ (q_1q_2,a)=1}}\Bigl|\mathop{\sideset{}{^*}\sum}_{\substack{p_1,\dots,p_J\\ p_i\sim P_i\forall i}}S_{p_1\cdots p_J}\Bigr|\ll_{A}\frac{x}{(\log{x})^A}. \] Here $\sum^*$ indicates that the summation is restricted by $O(1)$ inequalities of the form $p_1^{\alpha_1}\cdots p_J^{\alpha_J}\le B$. The implied constant may depend on all such exponents $\alpha_i$, but none of the quantities $B$.
assumptions: $P_1,\dots, P_J\ge x^{1/7+10\epsilon}$ be such that $P_1\cdots P_J\asymp x$
conclusions: \sum_{q_1\sim Q_1}\sum_{\substack{q_2\sim Q_2\\ (q_1q_2,a)=1}}\Bigl|\mathop{\sideset{}{^*}\sum}_{\substack{p_1,\dots,p_J\\ p_i\sim P_i\forall i}}S_{p_1\cdots p_J}\Bigr|\ll_{A}\frac{x}{(\log{x})^A}.
nodes.statement_short: Products of primes $>x^{1/7+10\epsilon}$ with a subproduct in $[x^{3/7+\epsilon},x^{4/7-\epsilon}]$ are equidistributed on average over $q_1q_2$.
nodes.label: prpstn:TypeII

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 7.1 assuming Proposition 8.1
nodes.statement: We note that $S_{p_1\cdots p_J}(p_J)$ is a weighted sum over integers $p_1\cdots p_J n\sim x$ with $P^-(p_1\dots p_J n)\ge x^{1/7+10\epsilon}$, and so with at most 6 prime factors. Expanding this into separate terms according to the exact number of prime factors, we see that each term is of the form considered by Proposition \ref{prpstn:TypeII}, and so the result follows immediately.
nodes.statement_short: Expand $S_{p_1\cdots p_J}(p_J)$ by number of prime factors; each term is covered by Proposition 8.1.

nodes.name: Zhang-style estimate
nodes.statement: Let $A>0$. Let $N,M,Q_1,Q_2\ge 1$ with $NM\asymp x$ be such that \begin{align*} Q_1^{12}Q_2^{7}&<x^{4-19\epsilon},\qquad x^\epsilon Q_2<N<\frac{x^{1-6\epsilon}}{Q_2}. \end{align*} Let $\beta_m,\alpha_n$ be complex sequences such that $|\alpha_n|,|\beta_n|\le \tau(n)^{B_0}$ and such that $\alpha_{n}$ satisfies the Siegel-Walfisz condition \eqref{eq:SiegelWalfisz} and $\alpha_n$ is supported on $n$ with all prime factors bigger than $z_0=x^{1/(\log\log{x})^3}$. Let \[ \Delta(q):=\sum_{m\sim M}\sum_{\substack{n\sim N}}\alpha_n\beta_m\Bigl(\mathbf{1}_{m n\equiv a \Mod{q}}-\frac{\mathbf{1}_{(m n,q)=1}}{\phi(q)}\Bigr). \] Then we have \[ \mathop{\sum_{q_1\sim Q_1}\sum_{q_2\sim Q_2}}\limits_{(q_1q_2,a)=1}|\Delta(q_1q_2)|\ll_{A,B_0} \frac{x}{\log^A{x}}. \]
assumptions: $\beta_m,\alpha_n$ be complex sequences such that $|\alpha_n|,|\beta_n|\le \tau(n)^{B_0}$ and such that $\alpha_{n}$ satisfies the Siegel-Walfisz condition \eqref{eq:SiegelWalfisz} and $\alpha_n$ is supported on $n$ with all prime factors bigger than $z_0=x^{1/(\log\log{x})^3}$
nodes.statement_short: Type II bilinear estimate for factorable moduli $q_1q_2$ when one factor $N$ lies between $x^\epsilon Q_2$ and $x^{1-6\epsilon}/Q_2$.
nodes.label: prpstn:Zhang

nodes.name: New estimate for triple convolutions
nodes.statement: Let $A,B_0>0$, $K L M\asymp x$, $\min(K,L,M)>x^\epsilon$, $a\ne 0$ and $x^{7/10-\epsilon}>Q>x^{1/2}(\log{x})^{-A}$. Let $L,K$ satisfy \begin{align*} Q x^\epsilon&<KL,\\ Q K&<x^{1-2\epsilon},\\ KL &< \frac{x^{153/224-10\epsilon}}{Q^{1/7}},\\ K L^{4}&<\frac{x^{57/32-10\epsilon}}{Q}. \end{align*} Let $\eta_k,\lambda_\ell,\beta_m$ be complex sequences such that $|\eta_n|,|\lambda_n|,|\beta_n|\le \tau(n)^{B_0}$ and such that $\eta_k$ satisfies the Siegel-Walfisz condition \eqref{eq:SiegelWalfisz}, and such that $\eta_k,\lambda_\ell$ be supported on integers with all prime factors bigger than $z_0$. Let \[ \Delta_{\mathscr{B}}(q):=\sum_{k\sim K}\sum_{\ell\sim L}\sum_{m\sim M}\eta_k\lambda_\ell\alpha_m\Bigl(\mathbf{1}_{k \ell m\equiv a\Mod{q}}-\frac{\mathbf{1}_{(k \ell m,q)=1}}{\phi(q)}\Bigr). \] Then we have \[ \sum_{\substack{q\sim Q\\ (q,a)=1}}|\Delta_{\mathscr{B}}(q)|\ll_{A,B_0} \frac{x}{(\log{x})^A}. \]
assumptions: Q x^\epsilon&<KL,\\ Q K&<x^{1-2\epsilon},\\ KL &< \frac{x^{153/224-10\epsilon}}{Q^{1/7}},\\ K L^{4}&<\frac{x^{57/32-10\epsilon}}{Q}.

$\eta_k,\lambda_\ell,\beta_m$ be complex sequences such that $|\eta_n|,|\lambda_n|,|\beta_n|\le \tau(n)^{B_0}$ and such that $\eta_k$ satisfies the Siegel-Walfisz condition \eqref{eq:SiegelWalfisz}, and such that $\eta_k,\lambda_\ell$ be supported on integers with all prime factors bigger than $z_0$
nodes.statement_short: Equidistribution of triple convolutions $\eta*\lambda*\alpha$ over all moduli $q\sim Q$ up to $x^{7/10}$ under four size conditions on $K,L$.
nodes.label: prpstn:TripleRough

nodes.name: Triple convolution of rough sequences
nodes.statement: Let $A,B_0>0$, $K L M\asymp x$, $\min(K,L,M)>x^\epsilon$, $a\ne 0$ and $x^{2/3-\epsilon}>Q>x^{1/2}(\log{x})^{-A}$. Let $L,K$ satisfy \begin{align*} Q x^\epsilon&<KL,\qquad K^3 L^2<x^{3/2-\epsilon},\qquad K^3 L^4< x^{2-2\epsilon},\qquad K^2 L^5 <x^{2-2\epsilon}. \end{align*} Let $\eta_k,\lambda_\ell,\beta_m$ and $\Delta_{\mathscr{B}}(q)$ be as in Proposition \ref{prpstn:TripleRough}. Then we have \[ \sum_{\substack{q\sim Q\\ (q,a)=1}}|\Delta_{\mathscr{B}}(q)|\ll_{A,B_0} \frac{x}{(\log{x})^A}. \]
assumptions: Q x^\epsilon&<KL,\qquad K^3 L^2<x^{3/2-\epsilon},\qquad K^3 L^4< x^{2-2\epsilon},\qquad K^2 L^5 <x^{2-2\epsilon}.
nodes.label: lmm:BFITripleRough

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 8.4
nodes.statement: This is \cite[Theorem 3]{BFI2} (with the roles of $K$ and $L$ reversed).
nodes.statement_short: Citation of BFI2 Theorem 3 with $K,L$ swapped.

nodes.name: Triple convolution involving a smooth sequence
nodes.statement: Let $A,B_0>0$, $ K L M\asymp x$ with $\min(K,L,M)>x^{\epsilon}$ and let $\beta_m,\eta_k$ be complex sequences with $|\beta_n|,|\eta_n|\le \tau(n)^{B_0}$. Let $\mathcal{I}_L\subseteq [L,2L]$ be an interval. Let $L,K,M$ satisfy \begin{align*} Q x^\epsilon&<KL,\qquad K^3Q<L x^{1-\epsilon},\qquad KQ^2<L x^{1-\epsilon}. \end{align*} Then we have \[ \sum_{\substack{q\sim Q\\ (q,a)=1}}\Bigl|\mathop{\sum_{k\sim K}\sum_{m\sim M}\sum_{\substack{\ell\in\mathcal{I}_L }}}\limits_{P^-(\ell)\ge z_0}\eta_k\beta_m\Bigl(\mathbf{1}_{k m \ell\equiv a\Mod{q} }-\frac{\mathbf{1}_{(k \ell m,q)=1}}{\phi(q)}\Bigr)\Bigr|\ll_{A,B_0} \frac{x}{(\log{x})^A}. \]
assumptions: Q x^\epsilon&<KL,\qquad K^3Q<L x^{1-\epsilon},\qquad KQ^2<L x^{1-\epsilon}.
conclusions: \sum_{\substack{q\sim Q\\ (q,a)=1}}\Bigl|\mathop{\sum_{k\sim K}\sum_{m\sim M}\sum_{\substack{\ell\in\mathcal{I}_L }}}\limits_{P^-(\ell)\ge z_0}\eta_k\beta_m\Bigl(\mathbf{1}_{k m \ell\equiv a\Mod{q} }-\frac{\mathbf{1}_{(k \ell m,q)=1}}{\phi(q)}\Bigr)\Bigr|\ll_{A,B_0} \frac{x}{(\log{x})^A}.
nodes.label: lmm:TripleSmooth

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 8.5
nodes.statement: This is \cite[Theorem 5*]{BFI2}.
nodes.statement_short: Citation of BFI2 Theorem 5*.

nodes.name: Combined triple convolution estimate
nodes.statement: Let $A,B_0>0$, $K L M\asymp x$, $\min(K,L,M)>x^\epsilon$, $a\ne 0$ and $x^{1/2-\epsilon/2}<Q<x^{127/224-10\epsilon}$. Let $L,K$ satisfy \begin{align*} Q x^\epsilon&\le KL\le x^{4/7-\epsilon},\qquad L\le K\le (L K)^{3/4}. \end{align*} Let $\eta_k,\lambda_\ell,\beta_m$ and $\Delta_{\mathscr{B}}(q)$ be as in Proposition \ref{prpstn:TripleRough}. Then we have \[ \sum_{\substack{q\sim Q\\ (q,a)=1}}|\Delta_{\mathscr{B}}(q)|\ll_{A,B_0} \frac{x}{(\log{x})^A}. \]
assumptions: Q x^\epsilon&\le KL\le x^{4/7-\epsilon},\qquad L\le K\le (L K)^{3/4}.
nodes.statement_short: Triple convolution estimate when $KL\le x^{4/7-\epsilon}$ and $L\le K\le (LK)^{3/4}$, combining Lemma 8.4 and Proposition 8.3.
nodes.label: lmm:TripleCombined

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 8.6 assuming Proposition 8.3
nodes.statement: We consider separately the cases when $K\in [L,(L K)^{5/8}]$ and $K\in [(L K)^{5/8},(L K)^{3/4}]$. If $L\le K\le (L K)^{5/8}$ we see that \begin{align*} K^3L^4+K^2L^5&\ll K^3L^4\le (KL)^{7/2}\le x^{2-3\epsilon},\\ K^3L^2 &\le (KL)^{2+5/8}\le x^{(4/7-\epsilon)\cdot 21/8}< x^{3/2-2\epsilon}. \end{align*} Thus Lemma \ref{lmm:BFITripleRough} gives the result in this case. If instead $(L K)^{5/8}\le K\le (L K)^{3/4}$ then $L\le (L K)^{3/8}$ so \begin{align*} Q K&\le x^{4/7-2\epsilon} (LK)^{3/4}<x^{1-2\epsilon},\\ KLQ^{1/7}&<(x^{4/7})^{8/7}<x^{153/224-10\epsilon},\\ K L^{4} Q&<(KL)^{17/8}x^{127/224-10\epsilon}<(x^{4/7-\epsilon})^{17/8}x^{127/224-10\epsilon} <x^{57/32-10\epsilon}. \end{align*} Thus Proposition \ref{prpstn:TripleRough} applies, giving the result in this case. This gives the result.
nodes.statement_short: Case split on $K$ versus $(LK)^{5/8}$: Lemma 8.4 in the first range, Proposition 8.3 in the second.

nodes.name: Split into two ranges
nodes.statement: We consider separately the cases when $K\in [L,(L K)^{5/8}]$ and $K\in [(L K)^{5/8},(L K)^{3/4}]$.
nodes.statement_short: Split according to $K$ relative to $(LK)^{5/8}$.

nodes.name: Case $K\le (LK)^{5/8}$
nodes.statement_short: Conditions of Lemma 8.4 hold.

nodes.name: Case $K\ge (LK)^{5/8}$
nodes.statement:
If instead $(L K)^{5/8}\le K\le (L K)^{3/4}$ then $L\le (L K)^{3/8}$ so
\begin{align*}
Q K&\le x^{4/7-2\epsilon} (LK)^{3/4}<x^{1-2\epsilon},\\
KLQ^{1/7}&<(x^{4/7})^{8/7}<x^{153/224-10\epsilon},\\
K L^{4} Q&<(KL)^{17/8}x^{127/224-10\epsilon}<(x^{4/7-\epsilon})^{17/8}x^{127/224-10\epsilon} <x^{57/32-10\epsilon}.
\end{align*}
Thus Proposition \ref{prpstn:TripleRough} applies, giving the result in this case. This gives the result.
nodes.statement_short: Conditions of Proposition 8.3 hold.

nodes.name: Divisor function bounds
nodes.statement: Let $|b|< x-y$ and $y\ge q x^\epsilon$. Then we have \[ \sum_{\substack{x-y\le n\le x\\ n\equiv a\Mod{q}}}\tau(n)^C\tau(n-b)^C\ll \frac{y}{q} (\tau(q)\log{x})^{O_{C}(1)}. \]
nodes.label: lmm:Divisor

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 8.7
nodes.statement: This follows from Shiu's Theorem \cite{Shiu}, and is given in \cite[Lemma 12]{BFI2}.
nodes.statement_short: Follows from Shiu's theorem; see BFI2 Lemma 12.

nodes.name: Heath-Brown identity
nodes.statement: Let $k\ge 1$ and $n\le 2x$. Then we have \[ \Lambda(n)=\sum_{j=1}^k (-1)^j \binom{k}{j}\sum_{\substack{n=m_1\cdots m_j n_1\cdots n_{j}\\ m_1,\,\dots,\,m_j\le 2x^{1/k}}}\mu(m_1)\cdots \mu(m_j)\log{n_{1}}. \]
nodes.label: lmm:HeathBrown

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 8.8
nodes.statement: See \cite{HBVaughan}.
nodes.statement_short: Citation of Heath-Brown.

nodes.name: Small sets contribute negligibly
nodes.statement: Let $\delta>0$, $Q\le x^{1-\epsilon}$ and let $\mathcal{A}\subseteq [x,2x]$. Then we have \[ \sum_{q\sim Q}\tau(q)\Bigl|\sum_{\substack{n\in \mathcal{A}\\ n\equiv a\Mod{q}}}1-\frac{1}{\phi(q)}\sum_{\substack{n\in\mathcal{A}\\ (n,q)=1}}1\Bigr|\ll x^\delta\#\mathcal{A}^{1-\delta}(\log{x})^{O_\delta(1)}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Discrepancy of a small set $\mathcal{A}$ summed over moduli is $\ll x^\delta\#\mathcal{A}^{1-\delta}$ up to logs.
nodes.label: lmm:SmallSets

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 8.9
nodes.statement: Trivially, we have that the sum is bounded by \begin{align*} \sum_{q\sim Q}\tau(q)\Bigl(\sum_{\substack{n\in \mathcal{A}\\ n\equiv a\Mod{q}}}1&+\frac{1}{\phi(q)}\sum_{n\in\mathcal{A}}1\Bigr) \ll \sum_{n\in\mathcal{A}}\tau(n-a)^2+\#\mathcal{A}\sum_{q\sim Q}\frac{\tau(q)}{\phi(q)}\\ &\ll \#\mathcal{A}^{1-\delta}\Bigl(\sum_{n\sim x}\tau(n-a)^{2/\delta}\Bigr)^{\delta}+\#\mathcal{A}(\log{x})^2\\ &\ll x^\delta \#\mathcal{A}^{1-\delta}(\log{x})^{O_\delta(1)}+\#\mathcal{A}(\log{x})^2. \end{align*} Here we applied Holder's inequality in the second line, and Lemma \ref{lmm:Divisor} in the final line. Since $\#\mathcal{A}\ll x$ this gives the result.
nodes.statement_short: Trivial bound plus H\"older's inequality and the divisor bound of Lemma 8.7.

nodes.name: Trivial bound and Holder
nodes.statement:
Trivially, we have that the sum is bounded by
\begin{align*}
\sum_{q\sim Q}\tau(q)\Bigl(\sum_{\substack{n\in \mathcal{A}\\ n\equiv a\Mod{q}}}1&+\frac{1}{\phi(q)}\sum_{n\in\mathcal{A}}1\Bigr)
\ll \sum_{n\in\mathcal{A}}\tau(n-a)^2+\#\mathcal{A}\sum_{q\sim Q}\frac{\tau(q)}{\phi(q)}\\
&\ll \#\mathcal{A}^{1-\delta}\Bigl(\sum_{n\sim x}\tau(n-a)^{2/\delta}\Bigr)^{\delta}+\#\mathcal{A}(\log{x})^2\\
&\ll x^\delta \#\mathcal{A}^{1-\delta}(\log{x})^{O_\delta(1)}+\#\mathcal{A}(\log{x})^2.
\end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Bound the sum trivially, then by H\"older.

nodes.name: Conclude via divisor bounds
nodes.statement: Here we applied Holder's inequality in the second line, and Lemma \ref{lmm:Divisor} in the final line. Since $\#\mathcal{A}\ll x$  this gives the result.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 8.7 and $\#\mathcal{A}\ll x$ give the result.

nodes.name: Separation of variables from inequalities
nodes.statement: Let $Q_1Q_2\le x^{1-\epsilon}$. Let $N_1,\dots, N_r\ge z_0$ satisfy $N_1\cdots N_r\asymp x$. Let $\alpha_{n_1,\dots,n_r}$ be a complex sequence with $|\alpha_{n_1,\dots,n_r}|\le (\tau(n_1)\cdots \tau(n_r))^{B_0}$. Then, for any choice of $A>0$ there is a constant $C=C(A,B_0,r)$ and intervals $\mathcal{I}_1,\dots,\mathcal{I}_r$ with $\mathcal{I}_j\subseteq [P_j,2P_j]$ of length $\le P_j(\log{x})^{-C}$ such that \begin{align*} \sum_{q_1\sim Q_1}\sum_{\substack{q_2\sim Q_2\\ (q_1q_2,a)=1}}&\Bigl|\mathop{\sideset{}{^*}\sum}_{\substack{n_1,\dots,n_r\\ n_i\sim N_i\forall i}}\alpha_{n_1,\dots,n_r}S_{n_1\cdots n_r}\Bigr|\\ &\ll_r \frac{x}{(\log{x})^A}+(\log{x})^{r C}\sum_{q_1\sim Q_1}\sum_{\substack{q_2\sim Q_2\\ (q_1q_2,a)=1}}\Bigl|\sum_{\substack{n_1,\dots,n_r\\ n_i\in \mathcal{I}_i\forall i}}\alpha_{n_1,\dots,n_r}S_{n_1\cdots n_r}\Bigr|. \end{align*} Here $\sum^*$ means that the summation is restricted to $O(1)$ inequalities of the form $n_1^{\alpha_1}\cdots n_r^{\alpha_r}\le B$ for some constants $\alpha_1,\dots \alpha_r$ and some quantity $B$. The implied constant may depend on all such exponents $\alpha_i$, but none of the quantities $B$.
conclusions: for any choice of $A>0$ there is a constant $C=C(A,B_0,r)$ and intervals $\mathcal{I}_1,\dots,\mathcal{I}_r$ with $\mathcal{I}_j\subseteq [P_j,2P_j]$ of length $\le P_j(\log{x})^{-C}$ such that
nodes.statement_short: Inequality constraints among the variables can be removed by restricting to short intervals, at a cost of a power of $\log x$.
nodes.label: lmm:Separation

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 8.10
nodes.statement: Clearly we may assume that $A$ is sufficiently large. We let implied constants in the proof of this lemma depend on $r$. By Lemma \ref{lmm:Divisor}, the set of $n_1,\dots,n_r$ with $n_i\sim N_i$ and $(\tau(n_1)\cdots \tau(n_r))^{B_0}>(\log{x})^{C_1}$ has size $\ll (\prod_i N_i)(\log{x})^{O_{B_1}(1)-C_1}$, and so by Lemma \ref{lmm:SmallSets}, if $C_1$ is chosen sufficiently large in terms of $A,B_0,r$ these terms contribute negligibly. After rescaling (and replacing $A$ with $A+C_1$), we see it suffices to consider the case when $\alpha_{n_1,\dots,n_k}$ is 1-bounded. We split the summation $n_i\sim N_i$ into $\lceil (\log{x})^C\rceil $ disjoint short intervals $n_i\in \mathcal{I}_{i,j}$ where \[ \mathcal{I}_{i,j}:=\Bigl[N_i+\frac{(j-1)N_i }{\lceil (\log{x})^{C}\rceil},N_i+\frac{j N_i }{\lceil (\log{x})^{C}\rceil}\Bigr) \] for $1\le j\le \lceil(\log{x})^C\rceil$. We see that $\mathcal{I}_{i,j}=[N_{i,j}, N_{i,j}+N_i/\lceil (\log{x})^C\rceil)$ for suitable $N_{i,j}\sim N_i$. We do this for each $1\le i\le r$, and so in total there are $O(\log^{Cr}{x})$ choices of these intervals. We clearly do not need to consider any tuple $(\mathcal{I}_{1,j_1},\dots,\mathcal{I}_{r,j_r})$ of intervals for which the inequalities implied by $\sum^*$ hold for no choice of $n_1,\dots,n_r$ with $n_i\in\mathcal{I}_{i,j_i}$. If the inequality $n_1^{\alpha_1}\cdots n_r^{\alpha_r}\le B$ can only hold for some but not all elements $(n_1,\dots,n_r)\in (\mathcal{I}_{1,j_1},\dots,\mathcal{I}_{r,j_r})$ then we must have \[ N_{1,j_1}^{\alpha_1}\cdots N_{r,j_r}^{\alpha_r}=B\Bigl(1+O_{\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r}\Bigl(\frac{1}{(\log{x})^{C}}\Bigr)\Bigr). \] If $\alpha_k\ne 0$, then, given a choice of $j_i$ for $i\ne k$, there are $O_\alpha(1)$ choices of $j_k$ such that the above holds. Thus there are $O_\alpha( (\log{x})^{C(r-1)})$ choices of tuples of intervals for which the inequalities hold for some but not all elements of the intervals. By Lemma \ref{lmm:SmallSets}, the total contribution from these $O_\alpha(\log^{C(r-1)}{x})$ tuples of intervals where the inequalities sometimes hold is $\ll_\alpha x (\log{x})^{O_\delta(1)-C(1-r\delta)}\ll_\alpha x(\log{x})^{-A}$ if we choose $\delta=1/(2r)$ and $C=C(A,r)$ large enough. Thus we only need to consider tuples $(\mathcal{I}_{1,j_1},\dots,\mathcal{I}_{r,j_r})$ of intervals where the inequalities hold for all choices of elements in the intervals. In particular, the inequalities can be dropped, and taking the worst tuple of intervals then gives the result.
nodes.statement_short: Discard large-divisor terms via Lemma 8.9, split variables into short intervals, and bound boundary tuples by Lemma 8.9.

nodes.name: Reduce to 1-bounded coefficients
nodes.statement: Clearly we may assume that $A$ is sufficiently large. We let implied constants in the proof of this lemma depend on $r$. By Lemma \ref{lmm:Divisor}, the set of $n_1,\dots,n_r$ with $n_i\sim N_i$ and $(\tau(n_1)\cdots \tau(n_r))^{B_0}>(\log{x})^{C_1}$ has size $\ll (\prod_i N_i)(\log{x})^{O_{B_1}(1)-C_1}$, and so by Lemma \ref{lmm:SmallSets}, if $C_1$ is chosen sufficiently large in terms of $A,B_0,r$ these terms contribute negligibly. After rescaling (and replacing $A$ with $A+C_1$), we see it suffices to consider the case when $\alpha_{n_1,\dots,n_k}$ is 1-bounded.
nodes.statement_short: Lemmas 8.7 and 8.9 remove terms with large divisor weights.

nodes.name: Split into short intervals
nodes.statement:
We split the summation $n_i\sim N_i$ into $\lceil (\log{x})^C\rceil $ disjoint short intervals $n_i\in \mathcal{I}_{i,j}$ where
\[
\mathcal{I}_{i,j}:=\Bigl[N_i+\frac{(j-1)N_i }{\lceil (\log{x})^{C}\rceil},N_i+\frac{j N_i }{\lceil (\log{x})^{C}\rceil}\Bigr)
\]
 for $1\le j\le \lceil(\log{x})^C\rceil$. We see that $\mathcal{I}_{i,j}=[N_{i,j}, N_{i,j}+N_i/\lceil (\log{x})^C\rceil)$ for suitable $N_{i,j}\sim N_i$. We do this for each $1\le i\le r$, and so in total there are $O(\log^{Cr}{x})$ choices of these intervals. 
 
 We clearly do not need to consider any tuple $(\mathcal{I}_{1,j_1},\dots,\mathcal{I}_{r,j_r})$ of intervals for which the inequalities implied by $\sum^*$ hold for no choice of $n_1,\dots,n_r$ with $n_i\in\mathcal{I}_{i,j_i}$.
nodes.statement_short: Split each $n_i$ range into $(\log x)^C$ short intervals.

nodes.name: Boundary tuples are negligible
nodes.statement:
If the inequality  $n_1^{\alpha_1}\cdots n_r^{\alpha_r}\le B$ can only hold for some but not all elements $(n_1,\dots,n_r)\in (\mathcal{I}_{1,j_1},\dots,\mathcal{I}_{r,j_r})$ then we must have 
\[
N_{1,j_1}^{\alpha_1}\cdots N_{r,j_r}^{\alpha_r}=B\Bigl(1+O_{\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r}\Bigl(\frac{1}{(\log{x})^{C}}\Bigr)\Bigr).
\]
If $\alpha_k\ne 0$, then, given a choice of $j_i$ for $i\ne k$, there are $O_\alpha(1)$ choices of $j_k$  such that the above holds. Thus there are $O_\alpha( (\log{x})^{C(r-1)})$ choices of tuples of intervals for which the inequalities hold for some but not all elements of the intervals. By Lemma \ref{lmm:SmallSets}, the total contribution from these $O_\alpha(\log^{C(r-1)}{x})$ tuples of  intervals where the inequalities sometimes hold  is $\ll_\alpha x (\log{x})^{O_\delta(1)-C(1-r\delta)}\ll_\alpha x(\log{x})^{-A}$ if we choose $\delta=1/(2r)$ and $C=C(A,r)$ large enough.
nodes.statement_short: Tuples where inequalities hold only partly are few; Lemma 8.9 bounds them.

nodes.name: Drop inequalities
nodes.statement: Thus we only need to consider tuples $(\mathcal{I}_{1,j_1},\dots,\mathcal{I}_{r,j_r})$ of intervals where the inequalities hold for all choices of elements in the intervals. In particular, the inequalities can be dropped, and taking the worst tuple of intervals then gives the result.
nodes.statement_short: On the remaining tuples the inequalities can be dropped.

nodes.name: Type II estimate away from 1/2 for convolutions
nodes.statement: Let $A>0$. Let $x^{1/2-\epsilon}\le Q\le x^{127/224-\epsilon}$, and let $M_1, \dots , M_r\ge 1$ be such that $\prod_{i=1}^r M_i\asymp x$ and \[ x^{\epsilon}Q <\prod_{j\in\mathcal{J}} M_j<x^{4/7-\epsilon} \] for some set $\mathcal{J}\subseteq\{1,\dots,r\}$. Let $\mathcal{I}_j\subseteq [M_j,2M_j]$ be intervals and $\beta^{(1)}_m,\dots,\beta_m^{(r)}$ be 1-bounded complex sequences satisfying the Siegel-Walfisz condition \eqref{eq:SiegelWalfisz}, supported on $m$ with $P^-(m)>z_0$, and such that $\beta_m^{(j)}=\mathbf{1}_{P^-(m)>z_0}$ for all $m>x^{1/15}$. Then we have \[ \sum_{\substack{q\sim Q\\ (q,a)=1}}\Bigl|\sum_{\substack{m_{1},\dots, m_{r}\\ m_{i}\in \mathcal{I}_i\forall i}}\Bigl(\prod_{1\le j\le r}\beta^{(j)}_{m_j}\Bigr)\Bigl(\mathbf{1}_{m_1\cdots m_r\equiv a\Mod{q}}-\frac{\mathbf{1}_{(m_1\cdots m_r,q)=1}}{\phi(q)}\Bigr)\Bigr|\ll_{A,r}\frac{x}{(\log{x})^{A}}. \]
assumptions: $x^{1/2-\epsilon}\le Q\le x^{127/224-\epsilon}$, and let $M_1, \dots , M_r\ge 1$ be such that $\prod_{i=1}^r M_i\asymp x$

$\mathcal{I}_j\subseteq [M_j,2M_j]$ be intervals and $\beta^{(1)}_m,\dots,\beta_m^{(r)}$ be 1-bounded complex sequences satisfying the Siegel-Walfisz condition \eqref{eq:SiegelWalfisz}, supported on $m$ with $P^-(m)>z_0$, and such that $\beta_m^{(j)}=\mathbf{1}_{P^-(m)>z_0}$ for all $m>x^{1/15}$
conclusions: \sum_{\substack{q\sim Q\\ (q,a)=1}}\Bigl|\sum_{\substack{m_{1},\dots, m_{r}\\ m_{i}\in \mathcal{I}_i\forall i}}\Bigl(\prod_{1\le j\le r}\beta^{(j)}_{m_j}\Bigr)\Bigl(\mathbf{1}_{m_1\cdots m_r\equiv a\Mod{q}}-\frac{\mathbf{1}_{(m_1\cdots m_r,q)=1}}{\phi(q)}\Bigr)\Bigr|\ll_{A,r}\frac{x}{(\log{x})^{A}}.
nodes.statement_short: Type II estimate for multiple convolutions with a subproduct in $(x^\epsilon Q, x^{4/7-\epsilon})$.
nodes.label: lmm:TypeIIAway

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 8.11 assuming Proposition 8.3
nodes.statement: After reordering the indices, we may assume that $\mathcal{J}=\{1,\dots,k\}$ with $M_1\ge \dots \ge M_k$. Define $N^*$, $N$ and $M$ by \begin{align*} N^*:=x^{1/14}Q^{1/2},\qquad N:=\prod_{j=1}^k M_j,\qquad M:=\prod_{j=k+1}^r M_j. \end{align*} Since $Q<x^{4/7-\epsilon}$ we have $N^*<x^{5/14}$, and since $\prod_{j=1}^r M_j\asymp x$ we have $N M\asymp x$. If $M_1\ge N^*$ then $\beta^{(1)}_{n_1}=\mathbf{1}_{P^-(n_1)>z_0}$, and we wish to apply Lemma \ref{lmm:TripleSmooth} with $L=M_1$, $K\asymp N/M_1$, $\gamma_\ell:=\mathbf{1}_{\ell\in \mathcal{I}_1}$ and \[ \eta_k:=\sum_{\substack{k=m_2\cdots m_{k}\\ m_i\in\mathcal{I}_i\forall 2\le i\le k}}\beta^{(2)}_{m_2}\cdots \beta^{(k)}_{m_{k}},\qquad \beta_m:=\sum_{\substack{m=m_{k+1}\cdots m_r\\ m_i\in \mathcal{I}_i\forall k+1\le i\le r}}\beta^{(k+1)}_{m_{k+1}}\cdots \beta^{(r)}_{m_r}. \] Since $M_1\ge N^*=x^{1/14}Q^{1/2}$ and $x^\epsilon Q< N\ll x^{4/7-\epsilon}$ and $Q\in [x^{1/2-\epsilon/2},x^{4/7-\epsilon}]$, we have \begin{align*} KL&\gg N> x^\epsilon Q,\\ K^3Q&\ll\frac{N^3Q L}{M_1^4}<\frac{x^{12/7} L}{x^{2/7}Q}<\frac{x^{10/7} L}{Q}<L x^{1-2\epsilon},\\ KQ^2&\ll \frac{N Q^2 L}{M_1^2}<\frac{x^{4/7-\epsilon} L Q}{x^{1/7}}<x^{1-2\epsilon}L, \end{align*} Thus Lemma \ref{lmm:TripleSmooth} applies, and this gives the result for $M_1 \ge N^*$. We now consider the case when $M_1<N^*$. We claim we can find a product of some of $M_1,\dots,M_k$ which lies in the interval $[N^{1/4},N^{1/2}]$. Since $N^*<N^{3/4-\epsilon}$, if $M_1\ge N^{1/4}$ then either $M_1$ or $M_2\cdots M_k\asymp N/M_1$ will lie in this interval. If instead $M_1<N^{1/4}$ then all of $M_1,\dots ,M_k$ are less than $N^{1/4}$, so choosing $j$ minimally such that $M_1\cdots M_j>N^{1/4}$ must give a suitable product (such a $j$ exists since $M_1\cdots M_k= N$). Thus in either case there is a product which lies in $[N^{1/4},N^{1/2}]$. After relabeling the indices $\{1,\dots,k\}$ (noting that this removes the property $M_1\ge \dots\ge M_k$) we may assume that $N^{1/4}\le M_1\cdots M_J\le N^{1/2}\le M_{J+1}\cdots M_k\le N^{3/4}$. We now consider $L\asymp M_1\cdots M_J$ and $K\asymp M_{J+1}\cdots M_k$ and \begin{align*} \alpha_m&:=\sum_{\substack{m=m_{k+1}\cdots m_r\\ m_i\in \mathcal{I}_i\forall k+1\le i\le r}}\beta^{(k+1)}_{m_{k+1}}\cdots \beta^{(r)}_{m_r},\qquad \lambda_\ell:=\sum_{\substack{\ell=m_1\cdots m_J\\ m_i\in\mathcal{I}_i\forall 1\le i \le J}}\beta^{(1)}_{m_1}\cdots \beta^{(J)}_{m_J},\\ \eta_k&:=\sum_{\substack{k=m_{J+1}\cdots m_k\\ m_i\in\mathcal{I}_i\forall J+1\le i \le k}}\beta^{(J+1)}_{m_{J+1}}\cdots \beta^{(k)}_{m_k}. \end{align*} We then see that since $L\le N^{1/2}\le K\le N^{3/4}$ and $L K\asymp N\ll x^{4/7-\epsilon}$ and $KL\gg N>x^{\epsilon} Q$, so Lemma \ref{lmm:TripleCombined} applies, giving the result for $M_1<N^*$. This finishes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: If the largest factor is big use Lemma 8.5 (smooth factor); otherwise group factors into $L\in[N^{1/4},N^{1/2}]$ and apply Lemma 8.6.

nodes.name: Define $N^*$, $N$, $M$
nodes.statement:
After reordering the indices, we may assume that $\mathcal{J}=\{1,\dots,k\}$ with $M_1\ge \dots \ge M_k$. Define $N^*$, $N$ and $M$ by
\begin{align*}
N^*:=x^{1/14}Q^{1/2},\qquad
N:=\prod_{j=1}^k M_j,\qquad 
M:=\prod_{j=k+1}^r M_j.
\end{align*}
Since $Q<x^{4/7-\epsilon}$ we have $N^*<x^{5/14}$, and since $\prod_{j=1}^r M_j\asymp x$ we have $N M\asymp x$.
nodes.statement_short: Reorder and set $N^*=x^{1/14}Q^{1/2}$, $N$, $M$.

nodes.name: Case $M_1\ge N^*$
nodes.statement:
If $M_1\ge N^*$ then $\beta^{(1)}_{n_1}=\mathbf{1}_{P^-(n_1)>z_0}$, and we wish to apply Lemma \ref{lmm:TripleSmooth} with $L=M_1$, $K\asymp N/M_1$, $\gamma_\ell:=\mathbf{1}_{\ell\in \mathcal{I}_1}$ and
\[
\eta_k:=\sum_{\substack{k=m_2\cdots m_{k}\\ m_i\in\mathcal{I}_i\forall 2\le i\le k}}\beta^{(2)}_{m_2}\cdots \beta^{(k)}_{m_{k}},\qquad \beta_m:=\sum_{\substack{m=m_{k+1}\cdots m_r\\ m_i\in \mathcal{I}_i\forall k+1\le i\le r}}\beta^{(k+1)}_{m_{k+1}}\cdots \beta^{(r)}_{m_r}.
\]
Since $M_1\ge N^*=x^{1/14}Q^{1/2}$ and $x^\epsilon Q< N\ll x^{4/7-\epsilon}$ and $Q\in [x^{1/2-\epsilon/2},x^{4/7-\epsilon}]$, we have
\begin{align*}
KL&\gg N> x^\epsilon Q,\\
K^3Q&\ll\frac{N^3Q L}{M_1^4}<\frac{x^{12/7} L}{x^{2/7}Q}<\frac{x^{10/7} L}{Q}<L x^{1-2\epsilon},\\
KQ^2&\ll \frac{N Q^2 L}{M_1^2}<\frac{x^{4/7-\epsilon} L Q}{x^{1/7}}<x^{1-2\epsilon}L,
\end{align*}
Thus Lemma \ref{lmm:TripleSmooth} applies, and this gives the result for $M_1 \ge N^*$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Lemma 8.5 with $L=M_1$.

nodes.name: Case $M_1<N^*$
nodes.statement:
We now consider the case when $M_1<N^*$. We claim we can find a product of some of $M_1,\dots,M_k$ which lies in the interval $[N^{1/4},N^{1/2}]$. Since $N^*<N^{3/4-\epsilon}$, if $M_1\ge N^{1/4}$ then either $M_1$ or $M_2\cdots M_k\asymp N/M_1$ will lie in this interval.
If instead $M_1<N^{1/4}$ then all of $M_1,\dots ,M_k$ are less than $N^{1/4}$, so choosing $j$ minimally such that $M_1\cdots M_j>N^{1/4}$ must give a suitable product (such a $j$ exists since $M_1\cdots M_k= N$). Thus in either case there is a product which lies in $[N^{1/4},N^{1/2}]$. After relabeling the indices $\{1,\dots,k\}$ (noting that this removes the property $M_1\ge \dots\ge M_k$) we may assume that $N^{1/4}\le M_1\cdots M_J\le N^{1/2}\le M_{J+1}\cdots M_k\le N^{3/4}$. We now consider $L\asymp M_1\cdots M_J$ and $K\asymp M_{J+1}\cdots M_k$ and
\begin{align*}
\alpha_m&:=\sum_{\substack{m=m_{k+1}\cdots m_r\\ m_i\in \mathcal{I}_i\forall k+1\le i\le r}}\beta^{(k+1)}_{m_{k+1}}\cdots \beta^{(r)}_{m_r},\qquad \lambda_\ell:=\sum_{\substack{\ell=m_1\cdots m_J\\ m_i\in\mathcal{I}_i\forall 1\le i \le J}}\beta^{(1)}_{m_1}\cdots \beta^{(J)}_{m_J},\\
\eta_k&:=\sum_{\substack{k=m_{J+1}\cdots m_k\\ m_i\in\mathcal{I}_i\forall J+1\le i \le k}}\beta^{(J+1)}_{m_{J+1}}\cdots \beta^{(k)}_{m_k}.
\end{align*}
We then see that since $L\le N^{1/2}\le K\le N^{3/4}$ and $L K\asymp N\ll x^{4/7-\epsilon}$ and $KL\gg N>x^{\epsilon} Q$, so Lemma \ref{lmm:TripleCombined} applies, giving the result for $M_1<N^*$. This finishes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Find a subproduct in $[N^{1/4},N^{1/2}]$ and apply Lemma 8.6.

nodes.name: Claim: a subproduct in $[N^{1/4},N^{1/2}]$
nodes.statement:
We claim we can find a product of some of $M_1,\dots,M_k$ which lies in the interval $[N^{1/4},N^{1/2}]$. Since $N^*<N^{3/4-\epsilon}$, if $M_1\ge N^{1/4}$ then either $M_1$ or $M_2\cdots M_k\asymp N/M_1$ will lie in this interval.
If instead $M_1<N^{1/4}$ then all of $M_1,\dots ,M_k$ are less than $N^{1/4}$, so choosing $j$ minimally such that $M_1\cdots M_j>N^{1/4}$ must give a suitable product (such a $j$ exists since $M_1\cdots M_k= N$). Thus in either case there is a product which lies in $[N^{1/4},N^{1/2}]$.
nodes.statement_short: Show some subproduct of the $M_j$ lies in $[N^{1/4},N^{1/2}]$.

nodes.name: Subcase $M_1\ge N^{1/4}$
nodes.statement: Since $N^*<N^{3/4-\epsilon}$, if $M_1\ge N^{1/4}$ then either $M_1$ or $M_2\cdots M_k\asymp N/M_1$ will lie in this interval.
nodes.statement_short: Either $M_1$ or the complementary product lies in the interval.

nodes.name: Subcase $M_1<N^{1/4}$
nodes.statement: If instead $M_1<N^{1/4}$ then all of $M_1,\dots ,M_k$ are less than $N^{1/4}$, so choosing $j$ minimally such that $M_1\cdots M_j>N^{1/4}$ must give a suitable product (such a $j$ exists since $M_1\cdots M_k= N$). Thus in either case there is a product which lies in $[N^{1/4},N^{1/2}]$.
nodes.statement_short: Take the minimal $j$ with $M_1\cdots M_j>N^{1/4}$.

nodes.name: Define $L$, $K$ and coefficients
nodes.statement_short: Relabel and define $\alpha_m,\lambda_\ell,\eta_k$.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 8.6
nodes.statement: We then see that since $L\le N^{1/2}\le K\le N^{3/4}$ and $L K\asymp N\ll x^{4/7-\epsilon}$ and $KL\gg N>x^{\epsilon} Q$, so Lemma \ref{lmm:TripleCombined} applies, giving the result for $M_1<N^*$. This finishes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 8.6 applies, finishing the proof.

nodes.name: Type II estimate away from $x^{1/2}$
nodes.statement: Let $A>0$ and $Q_1Q_2\le x^{127/224-\epsilon}$, and let $P_1,\dots, P_J\ge x^{1/7+10\epsilon}$ be such that $P_1\cdots P_J\asymp x$ and \[ x^{\epsilon}Q_1Q_2 <\prod_{j\in\mathcal{J}}P_j<x^{4/7-\epsilon} \] for some subset $\mathcal{J}\subseteq\{1,\dots,J\}$. Then we have \[ \sum_{q_1\sim Q_1}\sum_{\substack{q_2\sim Q_2\\ (q_1q_2,a)=1}}\Bigl|\mathop{\sideset{}{^*}\sum}_{\substack{p_1,\dots,p_J\\ p_i\sim P_i\forall i}}S_{p_1\cdots p_J}\Bigr|\ll_{A}\frac{x}{(\log{x})^A}. \] Here $\sum^*$ indicates that the summation is restricted by $O(1)$ inequalities of the form $p_1^{\alpha_1}\cdots p_J^{\alpha_J}\le B$. The implied constant may depend on all such exponents $\alpha_i$, but none of the quantities $B$.
assumptions: $P_1,\dots, P_J\ge x^{1/7+10\epsilon}$ be such that $P_1\cdots P_J\asymp x$
conclusions: \sum_{q_1\sim Q_1}\sum_{\substack{q_2\sim Q_2\\ (q_1q_2,a)=1}}\Bigl|\mathop{\sideset{}{^*}\sum}_{\substack{p_1,\dots,p_J\\ p_i\sim P_i\forall i}}S_{p_1\cdots p_J}\Bigr|\ll_{A}\frac{x}{(\log{x})^A}.
nodes.statement_short: Type II estimate for products of primes with a subproduct in $(x^\epsilon Q_1Q_2,x^{4/7-\epsilon})$.
nodes.label: lmm:BasicTypeII

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 8.12 assuming Proposition 8.3
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lmm:Separation}, it suffices to show for $B=B(A)$ sufficiently large in terms of $A$ \[ \sum_{q_1\sim Q_1}\sum_{\substack{q_2\sim Q_2\\ (q_1q_2,a)=1}}\Bigl|\sum_{\substack{p_1,\dots,p_J\\ p_i\in \mathcal{I}_i\forall i}}S_{p_1\cdots p_J}\Bigr|\ll_{B}\frac{x}{(\log{x})^{B}} \] for all choices of intervals $\mathcal{I}_1,\dots,\mathcal{I}_J$ with $\mathcal{I}_j\subset[P_j,2P_j]$. By splitting these intervals into sub-intervals of length $P_j(\log{x})^{-2B}$, and taking the worst such subintervals it suffices to show for every choice of $\mathcal{I}_1,\dots, \mathcal{I}_J$ with $\mathcal{I}_j\subseteq[P_j,2P_j]$ of length $P_j(\log{x})^{-2B}$ that \[ \sum_{q_1\sim Q_1}\sum_{\substack{q_2\sim Q_2\\ (q_1q_2,a)=1}}\Bigl|\sum_{\substack{p_1,\dots,p_J\\ p_i\in \mathcal{I}_i\forall i}}S_{p_1\cdots p_J}\Bigr|\ll_{B}\frac{x}{(\log{x})^{(2J+1)B}}. \] For $p_j\in [N_j,N_j+N_j(\log{x})^{-2B})$ we see that $\Lambda(p_j)=\log{N_j}+O((\log{x})^{-2B})$. Since $J\le 6$ and $B$ is sufficiently large, Lemma \ref{lmm:SmallSets} shows that the error term contributes \[ \ll (\log{x})^{-2B}\frac{x}{(\log{x})^{2 J B(1-\epsilon)-O(1)}}\ll \frac{x}{(\log{x})^{(2J+1)B}}, \] which is acceptable. Similarly, by Lemma \ref{lmm:SmallSets}, higher prime-powers contribute negligibly, and so we may replace the sum over primes with a sum of $\mathbf{1}_{P^-(n)>z_0}\Lambda(n)/\log{N_j}$ over integers $n\in\mathcal{I}_j$. Thus it suffices to show that \[ \sum_{q_1\sim Q_1}\sum_{\substack{q_2\sim Q_2\\ (q_1q_2,a)=1}}\Bigl|\sum_{\substack{n_1,\dots,n_J\\ n_i\in \mathcal{I}_i\forall i\\ P^-(n_i)>z_0\forall i}}\Lambda(n_1)\cdots \Lambda(n_J) S_{n_1\cdots n_j}\Bigr|\ll_{B}\frac{x}{(\log{x})^{(2J+1)B}}. \] We now apply Lemma \ref{lmm:HeathBrown} with $k=20$ to expand $\Lambda(n)$ into a sum over new variables, and we put the new variables into dyadic intervals $[M_{i,j},2M_{i,j})$. Thus it suffices to show that for a suitable constant $C$ sufficiently large in terms of $B$ \[ \sum_{q_1\sim Q_1}\sum_{\substack{q_2\sim Q_2\\ (q_1q_2,a)=1}}\Bigl|\sum_{\substack{m_{1,1},\dots, m_{J,40}\\ m_{i,j}\sim M_{i,j}\,\forall i,j\\ \prod_{j=1}^{40} m_{i,j}\in \mathcal{I}_i\forall i\\ P^-(m_{i,j})>z_0\forall i,j}}\Bigl(\prod_{\substack{1\le i\le J\\ 1\le j\le 40}}\alpha_{m_{i,j}}^{(j)}\Bigr) S_{m_{1,1}\cdots m_{J,40}}\Bigr|\ll_{C}\frac{x}{(\log{x})^{C}}. \] where $M_{i,j}\le x^{1/20}$ for $j\le 20$ and \[ \alpha^{(j)}_m=\begin{cases} \mu(m),\qquad &\text{if }j\le 20,\\ \log{m},&\text{if }j=21,\\ 1,&\text{if }22\le j\le 40. \end{cases} \] By applying Lemma \ref{lmm:Separation} again, we can remove the conditions $\prod_{j=1}^{40}m_{i,j}\in\mathcal{I}_i$. Thus we see it suffices to show that for every choice of $M_{i,j}$ with $M_{i,j}\ll x^{1/20}$ if $j\le 20$ and $\prod_{j=1}^{40} M_{i,j}\asymp P_i$ and for every choice of intervals $\mathcal{I}'_{i,j}\subseteq[M_{i,j},2M_{i,j}]$ and every $C>0$ we have \[ \sum_{q_1\sim Q_1}\sum_{\substack{q_2\sim Q_2\\ (q_1q_2,a)=1}}\Bigl|\sum_{\substack{m_{1,1},\dots, m_{J,40}\\ m_{i,j}\in \mathcal{I}'_{i,j}\,\forall i,j\\ P^-(m_{i,j})>z_0\forall i,j }}\Bigl(\prod_{\substack{1\le i\le J\\ 1\le j\le 40}}\alpha_{m_{i,j}}^{(j)}\Bigr) S_{m_{1,1}\cdots m_{J,40}}\Bigr|\ll_{C}\frac{x}{(\log{x})^{C}}. \] By splitting $\mathcal{I}'_{i,21}$ into shorter sub-intervals, we may replace $\log{m_{i,21}}$ by a constant depending only on the subinterval in exactly the same way we saw that $\Lambda(p_i)$ was essentially constant on these short intervals. Therefore, it suffices to show for every $C>0$ \[ \sum_{q_1\sim Q_1}\sum_{\substack{q_2\sim Q_2\\ (q_1q_2,a)=1}}\Bigl|\sum_{\substack{m_{1,1},\dots, m_{J,40}\\ m_{i,j}\in \mathcal{I}'_{i,j}\,\forall i,j }}\Bigl(\prod_{\substack{1\le i\le J\\ 1\le j\le 40}}\tilde{\alpha}_{m_{i,j}}^{(j)}\Bigr) S_{m_{J,40}\cdots m_{1,k}}\Bigr|\ll_{C}\frac{x}{(\log{x})^{C}}, \] where $M_{i,j}\le x^{1/20}$ for $j\le 20$ and \[ \tilde{\alpha}^{(j)}_{m}=\begin{cases} \mathbf{1}_{P^-(m)>z_0}\mu(m),\qquad &\text{if }j\le 20,\\ \mathbf{1}_{P^-(m)>z_0},&\text{otherwise}. \end{cases} \] The result now follows from Cauchy-Schwarz (to replace the sum over $q_1,q_2$ by a sum over $q\sim Q\asymp Q_1Q_2$) and Lemma \ref{lmm:TypeIIAway}.
nodes.statement_short: Separate variables (Lemma 8.10), replace primes by $\Lambda$, expand via Heath-Brown's identity, and apply Lemma 8.11.

nodes.name: Separate variables
nodes.statement:
By Lemma \ref{lmm:Separation}, it suffices to show for $B=B(A)$ sufficiently large in terms of $A$
\[
\sum_{q_1\sim Q_1}\sum_{\substack{q_2\sim Q_2\\ (q_1q_2,a)=1}}\Bigl|\sum_{\substack{p_1,\dots,p_J\\ p_i\in \mathcal{I}_i\forall i}}S_{p_1\cdots p_J}\Bigr|\ll_{B}\frac{x}{(\log{x})^{B}}
\]
for all choices of intervals $\mathcal{I}_1,\dots,\mathcal{I}_J$ with $\mathcal{I}_j\subset[P_j,2P_j]$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 8.10 reduces to sums over intervals.

nodes.name: Shorten intervals
nodes.statement:
By splitting these intervals into sub-intervals of length $P_j(\log{x})^{-2B}$, and taking the worst such subintervals it suffices to show for every choice of $\mathcal{I}_1,\dots, \mathcal{I}_J$ with $\mathcal{I}_j\subseteq[P_j,2P_j]$ of length $P_j(\log{x})^{-2B}$ that
\[
\sum_{q_1\sim Q_1}\sum_{\substack{q_2\sim Q_2\\ (q_1q_2,a)=1}}\Bigl|\sum_{\substack{p_1,\dots,p_J\\ p_i\in \mathcal{I}_i\forall i}}S_{p_1\cdots p_J}\Bigr|\ll_{B}\frac{x}{(\log{x})^{(2J+1)B}}.
\]
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to intervals of length $P_j(\log x)^{-2B}$.

nodes.name: Weight by $\Lambda$
nodes.statement:
For $p_j\in [N_j,N_j+N_j(\log{x})^{-2B})$ we see that $\Lambda(p_j)=\log{N_j}+O((\log{x})^{-2B})$. Since $J\le 6$ and $B$ is sufficiently large, Lemma \ref{lmm:SmallSets} shows that the error term contributes
\[
\ll (\log{x})^{-2B}\frac{x}{(\log{x})^{2 J B(1-\epsilon)-O(1)}}\ll \frac{x}{(\log{x})^{(2J+1)B}},
\]
which is acceptable.
nodes.statement_short: $\Lambda(p_j)$ is nearly constant; Lemma 8.9 bounds the error.

nodes.name: Replace primes by von Mangoldt
nodes.statement:
Similarly, by Lemma \ref{lmm:SmallSets}, higher prime-powers contribute negligibly, and so we may replace the sum over primes with a sum of $\mathbf{1}_{P^-(n)>z_0}\Lambda(n)/\log{N_j}$ over integers $n\in\mathcal{I}_j$. Thus it suffices to show that
 \[
\sum_{q_1\sim Q_1}\sum_{\substack{q_2\sim Q_2\\ (q_1q_2,a)=1}}\Bigl|\sum_{\substack{n_1,\dots,n_J\\ n_i\in \mathcal{I}_i\forall i\\ P^-(n_i)>z_0\forall i}}\Lambda(n_1)\cdots \Lambda(n_J) S_{n_1\cdots n_j}\Bigr|\ll_{B}\frac{x}{(\log{x})^{(2J+1)B}}.
 \]
nodes.statement_short: Replace the prime sum by a sum of $\Lambda(n)$ over rough $n$.

nodes.name: Heath-Brown expansion
nodes.statement:
We now apply Lemma \ref{lmm:HeathBrown} with $k=20$ to expand $\Lambda(n)$ into a sum over new variables, and we put the new variables into dyadic intervals $[M_{i,j},2M_{i,j})$.  Thus it suffices to show that for a suitable constant $C$ sufficiently large in terms of $B$ 
 \[
\sum_{q_1\sim Q_1}\sum_{\substack{q_2\sim Q_2\\ (q_1q_2,a)=1}}\Bigl|\sum_{\substack{m_{1,1},\dots, m_{J,40}\\ m_{i,j}\sim M_{i,j}\,\forall i,j\\ \prod_{j=1}^{40} m_{i,j}\in \mathcal{I}_i\forall i\\ P^-(m_{i,j})>z_0\forall i,j}}\Bigl(\prod_{\substack{1\le i\le J\\ 1\le j\le 40}}\alpha_{m_{i,j}}^{(j)}\Bigr) S_{m_{1,1}\cdots m_{J,40}}\Bigr|\ll_{C}\frac{x}{(\log{x})^{C}}.
 \]
 where $M_{i,j}\le x^{1/20}$ for $j\le 20$ and
 \[
 \alpha^{(j)}_m=\begin{cases}
 \mu(m),\qquad &\text{if }j\le 20,\\
 \log{m},&\text{if }j=21,\\
 1,&\text{if }22\le j\le 40.
 \end{cases}
 \]
nodes.statement_short: Expand $\Lambda$ by Heath-Brown's identity with $k=20$ into dyadic ranges.

nodes.name: Separate again
nodes.statement:
By applying Lemma \ref{lmm:Separation} again, we can remove the conditions $\prod_{j=1}^{40}m_{i,j}\in\mathcal{I}_i$. Thus we see it suffices to show that for every choice of $M_{i,j}$ with $M_{i,j}\ll x^{1/20}$ if $j\le 20$ and $\prod_{j=1}^{40} M_{i,j}\asymp P_i$ and for every choice of intervals $\mathcal{I}'_{i,j}\subseteq[M_{i,j},2M_{i,j}]$ and every $C>0$ we have
 \[
 \sum_{q_1\sim Q_1}\sum_{\substack{q_2\sim Q_2\\ (q_1q_2,a)=1}}\Bigl|\sum_{\substack{m_{1,1},\dots, m_{J,40}\\ m_{i,j}\in  \mathcal{I}'_{i,j}\,\forall i,j\\ P^-(m_{i,j})>z_0\forall i,j }}\Bigl(\prod_{\substack{1\le i\le J\\ 1\le j\le 40}}\alpha_{m_{i,j}}^{(j)}\Bigr) S_{m_{1,1}\cdots m_{J,40}}\Bigr|\ll_{C}\frac{x}{(\log{x})^{C}}.
  \]
nodes.statement_short: Remove the product constraints with Lemma 8.10.

nodes.name: Remove the logarithm
nodes.statement:
By splitting $\mathcal{I}'_{i,21}$ into shorter sub-intervals, we may replace $\log{m_{i,21}}$ by a constant depending only on the subinterval in exactly the same way we saw that $\Lambda(p_i)$ was essentially constant on these short intervals. Therefore, it suffices to show for every $C>0$
   \[
\sum_{q_1\sim Q_1}\sum_{\substack{q_2\sim Q_2\\ (q_1q_2,a)=1}}\Bigl|\sum_{\substack{m_{1,1},\dots, m_{J,40}\\ m_{i,j}\in  \mathcal{I}'_{i,j}\,\forall i,j }}\Bigl(\prod_{\substack{1\le i\le J\\ 1\le j\le 40}}\tilde{\alpha}_{m_{i,j}}^{(j)}\Bigr) S_{m_{J,40}\cdots m_{1,k}}\Bigr|\ll_{C}\frac{x}{(\log{x})^{C}},
  \]
  where $M_{i,j}\le x^{1/20}$ for $j\le 20$ and
  \[
  \tilde{\alpha}^{(j)}_{m}=\begin{cases}
 \mathbf{1}_{P^-(m)>z_0}\mu(m),\qquad &\text{if }j\le 20,\\
 \mathbf{1}_{P^-(m)>z_0},&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
 \]
nodes.statement_short: Replace $\log m_{i,21}$ by a constant on short subintervals.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 8.11
nodes.statement: The result now follows from Cauchy-Schwarz (to replace the sum over $q_1,q_2$ by a sum over $q\sim Q\asymp Q_1Q_2$) and Lemma \ref{lmm:TypeIIAway}.
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy--Schwarz in $q_1,q_2$ and Lemma 8.11.

nodes.name: Type II estimate near 1/2
nodes.statement: Let $A>0$ and let $Q_1,Q_2$ satisfy \eqref{eq:Cons1} and \eqref{eq:Cons2}. Let $P_1,\dots,P_J\ge x^{1/7+10\epsilon}$ be such that $P_1\cdots P_J\asymp x$ and \[ \frac{x^{1-\epsilon}}{Q_1Q_2}\le \prod_{j\in \mathcal{J}}P_j\le x^\epsilon Q_1Q_2, \] for some subset $\mathcal{J}\subseteq\{1,\dots,J\}$. Then we have \[ \sum_{q_1\sim Q_1}\sum_{\substack{q_2\sim Q_2\\ (q_1q_2,a)=1}}\Bigl|\mathop{\sideset{}{^*}\sum}_{\substack{p_1,\dots,p_J\\ p_i\sim P_i\,\forall i}}S_{p_1\cdots p_J}\Bigr|\ll_A\frac{x}{(\log{x})^A}. \] Here $\sum^*$ indicates that the summation is restricted by $O(1)$ inequalities of the form $p_1^{\alpha_1}\cdots p_J^{\alpha_J}\le B$. The implied constant may depend on all such exponents $\alpha_i$, but none of the quantities $B$.
assumptions: $P_1,\dots,P_J\ge x^{1/7+10\epsilon}$ be such that $P_1\cdots P_J\asymp x$
conclusions: \sum_{q_1\sim Q_1}\sum_{\substack{q_2\sim Q_2\\ (q_1q_2,a)=1}}\Bigl|\mathop{\sideset{}{^*}\sum}_{\substack{p_1,\dots,p_J\\ p_i\sim P_i\,\forall i}}S_{p_1\cdots p_J}\Bigr|\ll_A\frac{x}{(\log{x})^A}.
nodes.statement_short: Type II estimate when a subproduct lies within $x^{\epsilon}$-ish of $x^{1/2}$, via the Zhang-style estimate.
nodes.label: lmm:ZhangTypeII

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 8.13 assuming Proposition 8.2
nodes.statement: This follows quickly from Proposition \ref{prpstn:Zhang}. Indeed, by Lemma \ref{lmm:Separation}, it suffices to show that \[ \sum_{q_1\sim Q_1}\sum_{\substack{q_2\sim Q_2\\ (q_1q_2,a)=1}}\Bigl|\sum_{\substack{p_1,\dots,p_J\\ p_i\in \mathcal{I}_i\forall i}}S_{p_1\cdots p_J}\Bigr|\ll_{B}\frac{x}{(\log{x})^{B}}. \] for every $B>0$ and every choice of intervals $\mathcal{I}_1,\dots,\mathcal{I}_J$ with $\mathcal{I}_j\subset[P_j,2P_j]$. By reordering the indices, we may assume $\mathcal{J}=\{1,\dots,k\}$. By considering $N\asymp \prod_{j=1}^k P_j$, and $M\asymp \prod_{j=k+1}^{J}P_j$ and \[ \alpha_n:=\sum_{\substack{n=p_1\cdots p_k\\ p_i\in \mathcal{I}_i}}1,\qquad \beta_m:=\sum_{\substack{m=p_{k+1}\cdots p_J\\ p_i\in \mathcal{I}_i}}1, \] we see that Proposition \ref{prpstn:Zhang} gives the result in the range \[ Q_2x^\epsilon<N<\frac{x^{1-7\epsilon}}{Q_2} \] provided \eqref{eq:Cons2} holds. This covers the range $x^{1-\epsilon}/(Q_1Q_2)<N\le x^\epsilon Q_1 Q_2$ provided \begin{align*} Q_1Q_2^2&<x^{1-16\epsilon}. \end{align*} This is condition \eqref{eq:Cons1}, and so gives the result.
nodes.statement_short: Separate variables and apply Proposition 8.2 with $N$ the product over $\mathcal{J}$; conditions reduce to (1.3)--(1.4).

nodes.name: Separate variables
nodes.statement:
This follows quickly from Proposition \ref{prpstn:Zhang}. Indeed, by Lemma \ref{lmm:Separation}, it suffices to show that
\[
\sum_{q_1\sim Q_1}\sum_{\substack{q_2\sim Q_2\\ (q_1q_2,a)=1}}\Bigl|\sum_{\substack{p_1,\dots,p_J\\ p_i\in \mathcal{I}_i\forall i}}S_{p_1\cdots p_J}\Bigr|\ll_{B}\frac{x}{(\log{x})^{B}}.
\]
for every $B>0$ and every choice of intervals $\mathcal{I}_1,\dots,\mathcal{I}_J$ with $\mathcal{I}_j\subset[P_j,2P_j]$.

\[
\alpha_n:=\sum_{\substack{n=p_1\cdots p_k\\ p_i\in \mathcal{I}_i}}1,\qquad \beta_m:=\sum_{\substack{m=p_{k+1}\cdots p_J\\ p_i\in \mathcal{I}_i}}1,
\]
we see that Proposition \ref{prpstn:Zhang} gives the result in the range
\[
Q_2x^\epsilon<N<\frac{x^{1-7\epsilon}}{Q_2}

provided \eqref{eq:Cons2} holds.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 8.1 assuming Propositions 8.2 and 8.3
nodes.statement: This follows immediately from Lemma \ref{lmm:BasicTypeII} and Lemma \ref{lmm:ZhangTypeII}, noting that \eqref{eq:Cons1} and \eqref{eq:Cons2} imply that $Q_1Q_2=(Q_1Q_2^2)^{5/17}(Q_1^{12}Q_2^{7})^{1/17}<x^{9/17}<x^{127/224-\epsilon}$.
nodes.statement_short: Combine Lemmas 8.12 and 8.13, using $Q_1Q_2<x^{9/17}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 7.3 assuming Propositions 8.1 and 8.3
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lmm:Separation} (and adjusting the constant $A$ suitably), it suffices to show for every choice of $\mathcal{I}_1,\dots,\mathcal{I}_J$ with $\mathcal{I}_j\subseteq[P_j,2P_j]$ and every choice of $A>0$ that \[ \sum_{q_1\sim Q_1}\sum_{\substack{q_2\sim Q_2\\ (q_1q_2,a)=1}}\Bigl|\sum_{\substack{p_1,\dots,p_J\\ p_i\in \mathcal{I}_i\forall i}}S_{p_1\cdots p_J}\Bigr|\ll_{A}\frac{x}{(\log{x})^A}. \] We first note that from \eqref{eq:Cons1} and \eqref{eq:Cons2} we have \[ Q_1Q_2=(Q_1Q_2^2)^{5/17}(Q_1^{12}Q_2^{7})^{1/17}<x^{9/17}. \] Since $P_i>x^{1/7+10\epsilon}$ and $P_1\cdots P_J\ll x$ we have that $J\le 6$. By assumption $J\ge 4$. We split the argument into 3 cases depending on whether $J=4,5$ or $6$. \medskip \textbf{Case 1: $J=4$.} Since $P_i\ge x^{1/7+10\epsilon}$ for all $i$, we have that $P_2P_3P_4>x^{3/7+\epsilon}$, so the result follows from Proposition \ref{prpstn:TypeII} unless $P_2P_3P_4>x^{4/7-\epsilon}$. Thus we may assume $P_1<x^{3/7+\epsilon}$. Similarly, we have $P_1P_4>(P_1P_2P_3P_4)^{1/3}P_4^{2/3}\gg x^{1/3}x^{2/21+20\epsilon/3}>x^{3/7+\epsilon}$, so we are also done by Proposition \ref{prpstn:TypeII} unless $P_1P_4>x^{4/7-\epsilon}$. We now wish to apply Proposition \ref{prpstn:TripleRough}. We let $K=\min(P_1,P_2P_3)$, $L=P_4$, $M\asymp x/KL\asymp\max(P_1,P_2P_3)$. If $P_1\le P_2P_3$ we choose \[ \eta_k:=\sum_{\substack{p_1=k\\ p_1\in\mathcal{I}_1}}1,\qquad \lambda_\ell:=\sum_{\substack{p_4=\ell\\ p_4\in\mathcal{I}_4}}1,\qquad\alpha_m:=\sum_{\substack{m=p_2p_3\\ p_2\in\mathcal{I}_2\\ p_3\in\mathcal{I}_3}}1, \] whereas if $P_1>P_2P_3$ we swap the definitions of $\eta_k$ and $\alpha_m$. Since $P_4\le \dots \le P_1\le x^{3/7+\epsilon}$, $P_1P_4>x^{4/7-\epsilon}$ and $Q_1Q_2<x^{9/13}<x^{4/7-5\epsilon}$, we have \begin{align*} K L&=\min(P_1 P_4,P_2P_3P_4)>x^{4/7-\epsilon}>x^{2\epsilon} Q_1 Q_2,\\ K Q_1Q_2&<x^{3/7+\epsilon}x^{4/7-5\epsilon}<x^{1-2\epsilon}.\\ (Q_1Q_2)^{1/7} K L&<x^{4/49} P_1^{3/5}(P_2P_3)^{2/5}P_4^{3/5} (P_2P_3)^{1/5}\ll x^{3/5+4/49}<x^{153/224-10\epsilon},\\ (Q_1Q_2) K L^{4}&<x^{9/17}P_1P_4(P_2P_3)^{3/2}\ll x^{9/17+1+3/14}<x^{57/32-10\epsilon}. \end{align*} Thus Proposition \ref{prpstn:TripleRough} applies, giving the result. \medskip \textbf{Case 2: $J=5$.} Since $P_i\ge x^{1/7+10\epsilon}$ for all $i$, we have that $P_3P_4P_5>x^{3/7+\epsilon}$, so the result follows from Proposition \ref{prpstn:TypeII} unless $P_3P_4P_5>x^{4/7-\epsilon}$. We now wish to apply Proposition \ref{prpstn:TripleRough} with $K\asymp P_4 P_5$, $L=P_3$ and $M\asymp P_1P_2$ and \begin{align*} \eta_k:=\sum_{\substack{k=p_4 p_5\\ p_4\in \mathcal{I}_4\\ p_5\in\mathcal{I}_5}}1,\qquad \lambda_\ell:=\sum_{\substack{p_3=\ell\\ p_3\in\mathcal{I}_3}}1,\qquad \alpha_m:=\sum_{\substack{m=p_1p_2\\ p_1\in\mathcal{I}_1\\ p_2\in\mathcal{I}_2}}1. \end{align*} We see that since $P_5\le P_4\le P_3\le P_2\le P_1$, $P_3 P_4 P_5>x^{4/7-\epsilon}$ and $Q_1Q_2<x^{9/17-5\epsilon}$ we have \begin{align*} Q_1Q_2 x^{2\epsilon}&<x^{4/7-\epsilon}<P_3 P_4 P_5 \ll L K,\\ Q_1Q_2 K&<x^{4/7}(P_1P_2P_3P_4P_5)^{2/5}\ll x^{34/35}<x^{1-2\epsilon},\\ (Q_1Q_2)^{1/7} K L&<x^{4/49}(P_1P_2P_3P_4P_5)^{3/5}\ll x^{3/5+4/49}<x^{153/224-10\epsilon},\\ Q_1Q_2 K L^{4}&<x^{9/17}\frac{(P_1P_2P_3P_4P_5)^{4/3}}{(P_4P_5)^{1/3}}\ll x^{9/17+4/3-2/7\cdot 1/3}<x^{57/32-10\epsilon}. \end{align*} Thus all the conditions of Proposition \ref{prpstn:TripleRough} are satisfied, and so Proposition \ref{prpstn:TripleRough} gives the result. \medskip \textbf{Case 3: $J=6$.} Since all the $P_i$ are at least $x^{1/7+10\epsilon}$ in size, we see that the product of any three of them is of size at least $x^{3/7+2\epsilon}$. But then we must have $P_1P_2P_3\in [x^{3/7+\epsilon},x^{4/7-\epsilon}]$, since $P_1P_2P_3,P_4P_5P_6>x^{3/7+2\epsilon}$ and $P_1P_2P_3\ll x/P_4P_5P_6$. Therefore we see that Proposition \ref{prpstn:TypeII} gives the result.

nodes.statement:
\textbf{Case 1: $J=4$.}

Since $P_i\ge x^{1/7+10\epsilon}$ for all $i$, we have that $P_2P_3P_4>x^{3/7+\epsilon}$, so the result follows from Proposition \ref{prpstn:TypeII} unless $P_2P_3P_4>x^{4/7-\epsilon}$. Thus we may assume $P_1<x^{3/7+\epsilon}$. Similarly, we have $P_1P_4>(P_1P_2P_3P_4)^{1/3}P_4^{2/3}\gg x^{1/3}x^{2/21+20\epsilon/3}>x^{3/7+\epsilon}$, so we are also done by Proposition \ref{prpstn:TypeII} unless $P_1P_4>x^{4/7-\epsilon}$.

We now wish to apply Proposition \ref{prpstn:TripleRough}. We let $K=\min(P_1,P_2P_3)$, $L=P_4$, $M\asymp x/KL\asymp\max(P_1,P_2P_3)$. If $P_1\le P_2P_3$ we choose
\[
\eta_k:=\sum_{\substack{p_1=k\\ p_1\in\mathcal{I}_1}}1,\qquad \lambda_\ell:=\sum_{\substack{p_4=\ell\\ p_4\in\mathcal{I}_4}}1,\qquad\alpha_m:=\sum_{\substack{m=p_2p_3\\ p_2\in\mathcal{I}_2\\ p_3\in\mathcal{I}_3}}1,
\]
whereas if $P_1>P_2P_3$ we swap the definitions of $\eta_k$ and $\alpha_m$.

\begin{align*}
K L&=\min(P_1 P_4,P_2P_3P_4)>x^{4/7-\epsilon}>x^{2\epsilon} Q_1 Q_2,\\
K Q_1Q_2&<x^{3/7+\epsilon}x^{4/7-5\epsilon}<x^{1-2\epsilon}.\\
(Q_1Q_2)^{1/7} K L&<x^{4/49} P_1^{3/5}(P_2P_3)^{2/5}P_4^{3/5} (P_2P_3)^{1/5}\ll x^{3/5+4/49}<x^{153/224-10\epsilon},\\
(Q_1Q_2) K L^{4}&<x^{9/17}P_1P_4(P_2P_3)^{3/2}\ll  x^{9/17+1+3/14}<x^{57/32-10\epsilon}.
\end{align*}
Thus Proposition \ref{prpstn:TripleRough} applies, giving the result.
